subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO TASK FORCE RECOMMENDATIONS ON TAX BENEFITS FOR NORTHERN AND ISOLATED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, it is my privilege today to present a petition rejecting the recommendations of the Task Force on Tax Benefits for Northern and Isolated Areas. Your petitioners, who represent the isolated community of Lebel-sur-Quevillon in Abitibi, are concerned about the recommendations in this report which may cause many workers to leave these isolated communities. They believe that the Government of Canada has refused to consider the fact that people in the north live in a harsh and isolated environment and that the cost of living is high.
Mr. Speaker, according to the disparity index for 84 isolated communities in Quebec in 1989, Lebel-sur-Quevillon ranks 70th and Fermont 81st.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my good friend from Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke put down a number of motions and of course this particular one would have us change the legislation so that some royalties would be collected from the two companies to be privatized, Nordion International Inc. and Theratronics International Limited, and that those royalties would be directed back to AECL.
There is a very good reason for that amendment. The people of Canada, the people who own those two companies through AECL which nurtured them in the early years before they improved their bottom line, ought to be the benefactors during some of the good times.
My colleague and I, and all my colleagues here in this caucus, do not think it is fair ball now to take those two companies and put them into the private sector without, in the process, providing some return to the people of Canada on the investment that they put into these two companies over the years. AECL could do with the

Government Orders
royalties and it could continue, in turn, to do the kind of work that it has been doing so well over the years.
There is another issue that needs to be addressed while we are talking about the old matter of privatization of those two companies. It is an issue that has come up in pretty well every legislative committee that we have had in this particular session of Parliament. That issue is the government's determination not to hear opposing views on the legislation.
My colleague and I, together with one member from the NDP and several from the Tory side, sat as a legislative committee on Bill C-13. It is a bill which has many ramifications. In its simplest form it would just privatize two companies, but that says it much too simply.
In the process it would put in private hands matters relating to food irradiation, for example. Across this country there are many people who have very legitimate concerns about the issue of food irradiation. We on the committee from this side of the House wanted to call some people who could enlighten the committee in terms of their concerns about food irradiation. My colleague and I had taken the step of being in contact with many people who wanted to appear before the legislative committee on Bill C-13.
They wanted to come and tell us, those who represent the people of Canada here in this place, some of their concerns: their safety concerns, their health concerns. People from the Canadian Cancer Society wanted to come and talk to us about the nuclear medicine issue which arises from this particular subject, for example. Do you know what the Tories did in that particular case? They did what they are doing in every single case without exception.
This is the same crowd which back in 1984 brought in some new rules to give members of this House a fuller opportunity in committee to ensure that legislation would be properly scrutinized. It would give a greater role for individual members from all across this country, yes, but in the process it would give the committees a greater role and, more to the point, it would better serve the Canadian people by ensuring that the legislation
proposed in this place which receives first and second reading is properly scrutinized in detail, clause by clause, before it comes to third reading and passage in this chamber.
That was the theory but something went wrong along the way. The government lost its commitment on this issue or, more to the point, decided it did not need the niceties of a committee procedure. So it now sends to committees its mobile gang, its group of parliamentary terrorists, almost, who come in every day with plugs in their ears and shut down the committees one by one, whether it is the committee addressing the question of clawing back seniors' pensions, the committee on Nor-dion, or any other committee for that matter.
I realize my time has run out so quickly, but there will be other opportunities. I appeal to all members of the House to do in this chamber what we were not allowed to do in committee because of the Tory majority: to say our piece, to express our concerns about nuclear medicine, about food irradiation and the other issues I would have got into had there been time.
Later in the day when we get to other amendments we will be up again, as I hope will every member of this chamber who shares these concerns.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, briefly on the amendment introduced by my friend from Renfrew-Ni-pissing-Pembroke, there has been a number of things raised in the comments on his amendment, the first being that we are trying to rush things through.
On March 4, 1988, almost two years ago, it was announced that Nordion and Theratronics would be divested from AECL and privatized. For the next year the work was done on these two companies to get them in shape for privatization. I had the privilege of introducing the legislation in this House on May 4, 1989.
At that time we had first reading. We went into second reading in June. The bill sat over summer, of course, and got into committee in October. I appeared before the committee and spent a considerable amount of time with my colleagues in committee answering their questions. I understand there were then motions in committee to put a time limit on the debate.
December 12, 1989

We are opposing this particular amendment, as my friend knows. I have chatted with him privately in this regard. AECL's future and its future funding is not related to the sale of Nordion and Theratronics in any way. I want to make it very clear that Nordion provided a very minor amount, I believe it was less than 5 per cent, of the funding for AECL. That is a separate issue that the minister of energy will address and is addressing at the present time, both the research and the development end of the Candu III, which we have heard a lot about and so on. Those statements will come from the minister of energy at another time and will be separate from what we are talking about here.
I must also comment on a couple of things that were said by my friends in opposition. One was that privatization is a Conservative ideology, that the Conservatives are hell-bent for election on privatization, and that it is strictly a Conservative bent.
If people look at what is going on in the world today they will see that communist countries are privatizing, socialist countries are privatizing, Liberal governments and countries governed by Liberals, God bless them, are privatizing, and Conservative governments are privatizing.
It is obvious that these various types of governments around the world have realized the benefits of corporations being held in private hands and run by the private sector, that in many instances these corporations can be better run and have better opportunities.
I wanted to make that point. I also wanted to point out that Nordion and Theratronics, being successful companies, will now be paying taxes to the federal coffers. We expect them to do extremely well in the private sector, so we would have to oppose this particular motion because AECL's funding requirements are not going to be solved by Nordion and Theratronics.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious debate that we are having on these two Crown corporations being privatized. The minister said that the sale of Nordion International and Theratronics International is not going to solve AECL's financial problems because I believe Nordion has been directing only 5 per cent of its revenue toward AECL in the immediate past.
I want to point out to the House and to all Canadians that that is 5 per cent more than this government has been willing to give. I also want to point out that Theratronics and Nordion together have had for 45 years taxpayers' money invested in them. The minister says that these companies are going to make a return to the taxation department of Canada because when they are privatized they will be paying taxes to the Government of Canada. That is nothing new. Every other company that starts from scratch pays taxes into the public Treasury of Canada.
But where are these two companies starting from? They have their factory in place. They have their sources of material in place. They have their marketing in place out there in the world. They have their technicians already in their plant. They have their engineers. They
have their specialists. They are starting from an ongoing successful operation.
The minister says that if we do not do this we are not going to give anything in return to the taxpayers of Canada. Both of these companies are predicted to grow considerably in the next few years.
The minister just said that everybody around the world is privatizing. Privatizing is one thing; the method of privatizing is another.
A large source of isotopes have been coming from the NRU reactor and the Chalk River nuclear laboratories. That NRU reactor is ageing. It will require repairs and indeed replacement. The Maple X reactor for the production of isotopes is still not on stream, and we do not know the time frame of when it will be coming on stream.
These amendments dealing with Theratronics were moved because there are no foreign control guarantees built into this bill. Nordion has a protection in this bill from foreign control. Theratronics has nothing. They have left it wide open because they want it to be flexible for investors.
We in this House all know what is going on today under the free trade agreement. We know what is going on in this particular case. If you are not going to put any controls on, then you must be looking for foreign investors. Are we going to stand idly by and allow this government to sell a Crown corporation off without any foreign controls on it after the taxpayers of Canada have brought that company to where it is today? There is an obligation here to deal with the taxpayers of Canada.
We hear often that when people buy things under privatization they have a right to profit, and that is quite true. Otherwise they cannot operate. If the taxpayers of Canada have an investment, should they not also have a return the same as any business?
The money for the sale of these two companies will be paid directly, as came out in the committee hearings, to AECL; but there is no guarantee that money is going to be left with Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. The government has already shown its hand. It has cut research and development by 50 per cent or $100 million in the 1985 budget of the Mulroney government. They lifted $70 million out of the reserve fund of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited.

When these companies are sold and the money paid to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited there is absolutely no guarantee-and this was said before our committee-that that money is going to remain there. They can lift it out and put it into the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, and heaven knows where it goes from there. We are into the ways and means of doing things here. The taxpayers of Canada are the ones who are going to be the losers.
AECL has had many years of research and development since 1952 on cancer research, Theratronics deals with the cobalt therapy unit for the treatment of cancer and all other related equipment. After 45 years of research, how can we tell a Crown corporation as large as Atomic Energy of Canada Limited today that it is going to be sold?
At a time when we are criss-crossing this country asking Canadians to donate money to the Canadian Cancer Society, we are going to sell off this program which has developed so much specialized treatment, R and D for cancer, to private enterprise with no return whatsoever to the parent organization. We say that this is wrong.
What is going to happen if Theratronics cannot be brought together under a Canadian ownership umbrella? "We are going to have a very flexible agreement or arrangement" says the government "in order to provide funds and provide buyers for Theratronics". Flexibility can mean that any American company, British company and so on can move in, buy up this Canadian taxpayer sponsored company and either stop production or take what they need to add to their own specialized product and Canadians no longer have control of it. There has to be control factors in here on both these operations.
That is the purposes of Motions Nos. 2, 3 and 4. Your Honour will notice that there is a whole host of changes in the bill. It simply means that wherever Nordion is mentioned in the bill-and there is protection built in for Nordion-we have applied through these amendments the same protection for Theratronics International on the production of cancer therapy units and related cancer equipment as we have in the Nordion company which produces the medical radio isotopes and irradiation for the industrial community. We feel very strongly about this point.
Government Orders
I want to make one comment before I sit down. I was very anxious to have the Canadian Cancer Society before the committee, but we all know what happened. Without even having one witness, not a single witness outside the presidents of the companies, the two unions of the companies, this government with its majority members in the committee and with the Minister of State for Privatization's legislative assistant sitting behind those members in the committee room, they moved a motion that witnesses not be heard and that we move clause by clause on the bill and report the bill back to the House. This government did not want the people of Canada to know what asset it was selling off. It did not want them to know that it is selling off and privatizing two companies which have done more for the treatment of cancer in this country than any other government agency, and at a time when we are asking people to donate to the Cancer Society of Canada.
I resent the fact that the government has run roughshod over the committee system in the House of Commons. This is only one example of it. Members of the government say that they are getting a hard time with this bill on the floor of the House. What can they expect if they are not going to let Canadians have their say before the committee and if they are not going to have any input from the members of parliament concerning the witnesses whom they want to appear before the committee? It is a good educational matter for all members of parliament and for the Canadian public to know what this government is selling off, to know what assets of ours it is selling off to private enterprise. It is not like any other company paying taxes. This company has all its organization in place from square one and it just takes off and buys a profit-making company.
Meanwhile the parent organization, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, will probably end up getting no return for the 45 years of research that has gone into that company. At the same time this government is saying to that Crown corporation, AECL: "You pay your own way because we are not going to give you any more money. You pay your own way, AECL, but we are going to sell off all your profitable assets". What kind of arithmetic and what kind of business planning is that? That is not business planning at all. That is selling off to your friends

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke has very clearly put before the House a serious gap which exists in this piece of legislation as it presently stands.
The logic of the government tells it with respect to Nordion to move ahead and put a 25 per cent restriction with respect to foreign ownership on this company. There is, however, absolutely no restriction with respect to Theratronics.
Theratronics is, in my view, in a slightly different category than Nordion. Nordion is a company which has shown an expansion over recent years which is quite dramatic. It is in a field in which the products which it produces are moving ahead with an ever-widening market evident before it. To talk about a 25 per cent restriction is sensible. It is very much consistent with what this government claims to be its commitment to Canadianization.
However, this commitment to Canadianization is equally important to recognize with respect to Theratronics. Theratronics is not a company which has as completely a rosy future as Nordion appears to have. Theratronics is a company which, frankly, operates with a technology which is not as close to the frontier, one which faces therefore a more difficult future. I think in a case like this it is proper to look for an arrangement
which stresses the Canadianization principle with somewhat less force than is true with Nordion. It is for that reason that I suggested the 49 per cent level.
Nevertheless, it seems to me that if one is prepared to take the principle of Canadianization and to put that principle into effect with one of these companies as it is privatized, then it is equally important to put that same principle into effect with the other company.
I agree that it is important to allow somewhat more flexibility, but to do so is one thing. To ignore the principle entirely, as this present piece of legislation does, is simply not to my mind a reflection of either government policy as it has been enunciated or of the logic which has been applied to Nordion in this very bill. Nor do I believe that it is consistent with the generally held views of most people across this country. While they may or may not be in favour of seeing the first case of a company in the nuclear industry being privatized, they certainly are not in favour of seeing us put this company into a position where it is possible for it to be lost to the Canadian people who have invested in the company and for it to become a privately foreign-owned firm. My subamendment provides sufficient scope to the employees of Theratronics to be able to work out some sort of a partnership if they feel that is necessary. That partnership will nevertheless be a partnership which remains under Canadian control. That is something which is extremely important, certainly to my mind.

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to say a few words on the subject.
I must admit that I have been following this issue perhaps not as closely as some other issues, but there is a logic with which I am concerned. It is a genuine concern. I am delighted that I have the opportunity to voice my concern. I am speaking on the amendments put forward by the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke.
Before we get to that, I do have to express my concern, which I think has been expressed by some of my other colleagues, about the general feeling about privatization of our nuclear industry. It is something I have always held dear, and I am certainly familiar with the background of atomic energy in Canada and the business of Canadians being in on the ground floor of this very important and key industry for the country. I was very

surprised when I saw that measures were being taken to privatize this key industry in Canada.
On the issue of this particular amendment put forward by my honourable colleague, I have a problem in following the logic put forward. I believe it is safe to say that Canadians watching this debate are wondering what on earth the members of Parliament are talking about What is the issue at stake here? What is being discussed?
What is being discussed is a sense of logic and certain inconsistencies that do not seem to have any reason or any basis. I think it is worth while to look at and to review the similarities between the two companies being privatized and what they do.
Both Nordion and Theratronics go back 45 years. They were created as divisions of Eldorado Mining and Refining. In the early 1950s they were transferred to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited.
On September 30, 1988, Nordion was incorporated and transferred to CIDC in anticipation of privatization. Nordion is primarily a radio chemical company and has two main lines of business, isotope products and industrial radiation.
Theratronics on the other hand does have the same background in the sense that it commenced operations in 1946 as part of Eldorado Mining and Refining, was transferred to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited in 1952 and, similarly, on September 30 of last year was incorporated as Theratronics International and transferred to the CDIC in anticipation of privatization. But Theratronics is an organization that is concerned primarily with medical products. I think a lot of Canadians know and appreciate that Theratronics was a pioneer in cancer treatment. It was responsible for designing the world's first cobalt therapy machine in 1951 just before its transfer to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited.
The point made previously by my hon. colleague for Essex-Windsor was that there are some dissimilarities between the companies. The one he was concerned about primarily, and I share his concern, was that Nordion because of its product and the way it is, and because of its gross sales and the number of people it employs shows some expansion possibilities. It shows possibilities that would lend itself to one set of conditions. On the other hand, my understanding is that Theratronics for a number of reasons is not considered
Government Orders
at this point in time to be on the cutting edge of technology. The general belief is that maybe the future is not as rosy as it is for Nordion. There is therefore a requirement for a Canadianization factor here.
Listening to my colleagues I was given to believe that there was some mechanical difficulty, or that there was some question of not co-operating, or maybe even a fluke of the committee system, but the Canadianization aspect of one company was not made as important as it was for the other. I am at a loss to really comprehend why this is so.
I look at the amendment that was put forward by my colleague for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke and, as I understand it, Motions Nos. 2, 3 and 4 relate to the several provisions to the sale of Nordion with regard to foreign ownership. These same provisions are not applied to Theratronics. I cannot understand why. I believe it should be so.
It is my firm belief that we should go forward in this regard and do whatever is necessary, whether it is a voting procedure, work of the committee, a deal that we can make behind closed doors, or some other way to deal with the Canadianization of this one company-indeed, the one that I believe needs Canadianization more than the other. We should move forward to approve these amendments to make sure this aspect is included in the consideration of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak in favour of the amendments proposed by my colleague to Bill C-13, an act to authorize the divestiture of Nordion International Inc. and Theratronics International Limited.
It is known that both companies were, until recently, unincorporated divisions of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, but that after incorporation the two companies were transferred to the Canada Development Investment Corporation as a prelude to privatization.
In May 1988 the president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited stated that AECL should realize some benefits from the sale of the two companies. These two companies have been seen as valuable properties. AECL had hoped the sale of both companies would help Atomic Energy of Canada Limited through a number of difficult years. The process occurred more slowly than

December 12, 1989

expected and is no longer controlled by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited.
The president was worried that AECL would be deprived of the cash flow of these companies and would not receive any compensation from the sales. I think on that basis the rationale for Motion No. 1 was proposed, which rationale I support.
For the past 45 years the federal government, and therefore the Canadian people, have invested a large amount of money into funding, research and development of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. The two companies we are discussing today have provided very profitable divisions for Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, and provided it with a cash flow which will be lost when these two companies are sold, unless we have guarantees of safety for the Canadian people.
In addressing Motions Nos. 2, 3 and 4,1 would like the same type of conditions to be imposed on the sale of Theratronics as would be on Nordion. Canadian control is desirable if we are to retain control of their policy. If these institutions have to be used as instruments of public policy, we have to ensure that ownership by Canadians to a great extent is retained. No similar restriction is evident in the current bill on the future ownership of Theratronics, hence my support for the amendments proposed by my colleague. In this way we can ensure that ownership is not transferred beyond Canadian hands.
The medical products division of Theratronics International Limited has the technological leadership in the design, installation and application of cobalt therapy equipment. Because it is involved with this type of therapy equipment it is essential that we maintain that ability to control policies so far as this company is concerned. If we were to leave it purely to the grace of foreign hands it may in fact threaten our ability to deliver essential medical therapy to patients with cancer in this country. That we must safeguard with all our might.
Theratronics, when separated from Nordion some three years ago, was earning some $40 million in revenue. The vice-president of the Medical Products Division says it could have a 30 per cent to 40 per cent growth in revenue in the next five years. We would not like to surrender profit. We would like it to remain in Canadian hands.
Theratronics' employees have been offered a priority opportunity to purchase the company. That would seem to be a welcome message. However, if the conditions thereafter are not clear in terms of being retained within Canadian control then this seemingly welcome sale of first opportunity to the employees would lose meaning in the future. If our will is to see to it that it remains in Canadian control then we must prescribe it in the bill through amendments as proposed by my colleague.
The other aspect that I would like to indicate to the House is that Theratronics' manufacturers are involved with the process of irradiation of food. Since there is a continuing debate as to the safety or non-safety of this process, I think we first have to settle that issue before we relinquish this to foreign hands and thereby lose control over this policy question. If there was a loss of regulatory control over these companies, foreign private buyers could take irradiation technology and impose irradiated food on Canadians or, in fact, citizens of the Third World beyond our control.
Canada has to play a moral leadership role on health care for the whole world and ensure that citizens of Third World countries may not be allowed to be guinea pigs in the future.
In conclusion, I support the amendments proposed by my colleague to protect the interests of Canadians who have contributed through our tax system to the development of the company in question; to ensure the viability of Atomic Energy Canada Limited and in fact prevent a continuing loss on the part of that institution; and to ensure that use and research and development of nuclear technology remain within Canadian control and therefore properly use this institution as an instrument of Canadian public policy.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am going to lead off the debate on third reading by first thanking my colleagues in the House, the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing, my hon. friend from Essex-Windsor, and also my colleague for Kingston and the Islands for their co-operation today in facilitating the minister in moving ahead on this very important bill. I do thank my colleague from Essex- Windsor, with whom I have had some very interesting times over the last few years, what with the free trade agreement and after being appointed a minister of the Crown, I found out that he is critic and I enjoy working with him very much. As he says, sometimes it is a little tense, but we do work well together. I want to thank them all for their co-operation.
We are at third reading of Bill C-13 which authorizes the divestiture of Nordion International and Theratronics. These former subsidiaries of Atomic Energy have made an impressive contribution to the advancement of medical science". Products and services provided by them are helping people around the world to live longer, healthier lives.
Nordion is a leading international supplier of industrial sterilization systems and medical diagnostic products. In addition, it is a major producer of radio isotopes and finished radio pharmaceuticals for international markets.
Theratronics produces and sells two main groups of products to radio-therapy clinics, Cobalt radio-therapy treatment and computerized treatment-planning equipment.
Both of these companies are export-oriented world-class companies in the vanguard of the nuclear medicine field. The new technologies pioneered by them have created sizeable market niches around the world for their products. To stay on the leading edge, however, they needed flexibility to respond or, better, anticipate a rapidly changing market-place. Transferring Nordion

Government Orders
and Theratronics to the private sector will help make them stronger, more flexible, and more competitive. It will give them access to new capital and the freedom to pursue new synergistic relationships that contribute to the long-term growth and stability. Nordion and Theratronics already have a private sector operating philosophy. They will benefit by the opportunity to exercise it freely.
I had the pleasure of visiting both these companies and of talking to the employees. They are very excited about this privatization and look forward to participating actively in it. Strengthening these companies will benefit the employees because, as has been said many times in this Chamber, the best guarantee of jobs and future prospects for employees is a dynamic and growing company. As well, a stronger Nordion and Theratronics benefits the country as a whole because their exports are important to our future economic development.
No valid reason exists that justifies continuing government ownership of either Nordion or Theratronics. The companies serve no public policy purpose. As for concerns about safety, a strict regulatory regime controlling all aspects of manufacturing, handling and transportation of radioactive material is in place in Canada. This will not change one iota with privatization.
The legislation we are considering today sets out certain conditions under which the divestiture will take place. These conditions are designed to protect employees' interests and to maximize the benefits to the company and to the Canadian public.
Nordion and Theratronics are different companies with different strengths. Because of this, it is our intention to proceed with a method of sale unique to each company.
In the case of Nordion, we intend to offer the company for sale to a third party. Our financial advisers have recommended this approach because it provides maximum benefits to the company in terms of stability of operations, access to new capital, the opening of additional markets through the purchaser, and the synergy of
relationship if the purchaser is in a similar or complementary business.
Theratronics is smaller and its market value is less than Nordion. It is as a result an appropriate candidate for an employee buy-out. To assist employees in developing a purchase proposal the government has offered to provide them with the necessary funding to hire financial advisers. It is our plan also to give their proposal priority before the company is offered to corporate purchasers.
I must point out that Nordion employees have also expressed an interest in purchasing an ownership interest in their company. They have similarly been assisted with funding to cover the cost of hiring advisers. They will, in addition, be given a 10 per cent discount on the purchase of a minority interest.
Since 1984 my government has worked hard to build a strong new foundation on which Canadians would achieve their economic potential. A number of structural policies and reforms have been introduced that have raised the prospects for growth and higher living standards for Canadians. Privatization is one of them. By transferring Nordion and Theratronics to the private sector, we are building for the future. I am proud to say that Canadians like what we are doing. Since 1984 our economy has expanded faster than most other industrialized countries, as a matter of fact, second only to Japan. More than 1.5 million jobs have been created, some
200,000	this year alone. Our economic strategy is obviously working. To assure that we continue to make economic progress, we must be steadfast in our goals in the face of those who prefer the status quo.
Nordion and Theratronics have the right stuff to become world leaders in the private sector. Bill C-13 gives them the chance to succeed. I want to wish both companies, their executives and, most importantly, their employees my best wishes for the future. I think they have an exciting future and Bill C-13 will help to guarantee that.

Mr. Speaker, it is rather interesting to have listened to the Minister who did not really at any stage talk about what these two companies actually do. I was wondering why he did not get into talking about the cancer therapy units, the medical radioisotopes and so on.

speechtext: I did.

You did on that one? All right, I thank you for that, but it was not really a blazing advertisement that I heard from over here.
The next question in all this, of course, is the future source of medical radioisotopes and the isotope market in general. The NR reactor at Chalk River is an old reactor and it produces our supply of isotopes today. It is rather scary that AECL is not being provided with a budget by this government to maintain the NRU reactor for this purpose. There are repairs going to be needed to it because it is becoming an older facility but we also have in the making a Maple X reactor which will be used exclusively for the production of isotopes. The original estimate of the cost of building the Maple X was $10 million five years ago, and the government has since updated that. Today it is going to cost about $35 million alone for that facility.
There has been an arrangement between Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Nordion International for the ongoing receipt from AECL of isotopes for the next 22 years. There is also a condition built into that which is the inclusion in this agreement of a provision that calls for Nordion to contribute $17 million through 1991 for new isotope production facilities.
The problem with the ageing NRU reactor has been identified. But my understanding is, and I have heard this talked about considerably, that the agreement signed between Nordion's previous personnel and Atomic Energy of Canada relating to this 22 years of guarantee of isotope production was done under pressure from the government because it wanted to sell these two profitable parts of the Atomic Energy Crown Corporation.
As a result, the agreement would show on the face of it that AECL will be losing money on that agreement for every one of those years. This is something that I would like the Minister to answer to. Is AECL going to continue to lose money every year on this agreement which now exists between Nordion and AECL for the production of isotopes and the receipt of them by Nordion? That is a 22-year guarantee.
If Atomic Energy of Canada is going to lose money on that agreement that was brought about under pressure from the government to sign it, then this again drains
Government Orders
funds away from the parent company, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Then the government's devastating program becomes two-fold. Number one, it says it is no longer going to finance AECL for R and D, that is must pay its way; and then is there indeed a loss of money each year for AECL on the agreement between Nordion International and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited? Those are the questions that the minister should answer today before the closing of this debate. He should state whether or not the government will revise that agreement to make sure that the user pays. The theory of this government is that the user must pay. So, since Nordion will now be the user of AECL, will the government make sure that it pays for that isotope production? The whole facility is in place throughout, the staff, factory and markets. It would be totally unfair to walk away and leave the parent Crown corporation with a loss in its own markets each year of that 22-year agreement.
Will the minister state to us today that he will see to it that Atomic Energy does, in fact, make money on that production when it sells or supplies isotopes to Nordion International? That is a very fair question because the government is after Ontario Hydro for greater contributions to the Crown corporation. So any products sold to any other organization or company in or outside of Canada should also more than pay its own way because it is obvious that this Crown corporation must have an income in the years to come.
It should be pointed out that Nordion has shown steady growth over the past four years and is projecting this trend to continue. It always had a good product to sell and has done very well. It has done well because it had an outstanding research and development facility on which to base its operations, namely the parent AECL operation.
The government says incorporation and transfer to the CDIC has had a positive effect on Theratronics, but it turned up in evidence in committee that Theratronics was making a profit before it was turned over to the Crown corporation CDIC. That should be pointed out because the government is trying to make people believe that this particular Crown corporation only became profitable after it had changed its status. That is not correct and there is no evidence to support it.

The amendment from the government today protecting Theratronics from foreign ownership and retaining ownership in Canadian hands is a big achievement.
In opposition you put forward your points and put motions on the Order Paper. With this majority government you know where you are going to end up. You are lucky if you get anything out of it. But in this particular deal a number of opposition members have taken up the cudgel and debated this bill very well. I want to congratulate my colleagues on the way they talked about this particular bill. I do not think the significance of the sale of Nordion International and Theratronics International, or what those two Crown corporations even stood for would have been known to many Canadians if this debate had not taken place.
Then, of course, we have that great theory in Canada projected by people who want to say that everything nuclear is bad. They try to relate it to nuclear weapons but there is no relation between the peaceful uses of the nuclear industry and war-time use. We must get that fact straight here in the House.
The reason I put forward the amendments on this bill and the reason we tried to highlight it becomes very obvious. It is time that we tried to educate everybody to the fact that if it was not for the CANDU reactors that have been produced by Atomic Energy of Canada over the years, there would be far more acid rain in the atmosphere than there is today.
You have heard me say it before, but I will repeat it for greater emphasis. This country would have had to spend more than $8 billion to buy coal from Pennsylvania to fire coal furnaces in this country to produce the same amount of hydro electric power in the Province of Ontario alone as has been produced over those years by the CANDU reactor. The CANDU reactor is indeed the safest one in the world. There is no relationship whatsoever to the structure of the one at Chernobyl. Of course, when there is an accident or someone who is not following the safety rules properly, it reflects on the whole industry.
It is the same thing in politics, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you have seen a few occasions over the years when one politician gets into trouble and every politician becomes condemned.
When one nuclear plant gets into trouble because people have neglected to do the right things and neglected looking after it properly or maybe the design was wrong in the first place, then every nuclear reactor becomes suspect. That is wrong and it is bad.
We have here in Canada this great base of technology in the CANDU reactor and in nuclear energy for peaceful purposes. In this Canada of ours, we have one of the greatest foundations to continue to build this nation industrially. And as there is the energy to supply factories, jobs are produced. Without energy, jobs cannot be produced. As well, we have the capacity to continue the growth of that industrial and commercial base and, indeed, the tourism base and all others, including agriculture. With this we will have the jobs that are coming on stream for the future, but more than that, and this is something that is not very often talked about, is the fact that there is the industrial base, the taxation income for government to help it control its finances, if it is capable of controlling them in the first place, and to pay for those very valuable social programs for senior citizens, veterans and for those other Canadians who cannot look after themselves. Surely, that is the social conscience of our nation.
I am very disappointed that the government did not relinquish some ground on the royalties issue, because the income coming back into the major corporation, AECL, is really what is going to continue that in depth research down the road. That is needed because a great research company such as this is not one that can be judged simply in dollars and cents. It produces a great variety of activity out there. These two companies are a perfect example of it. Then, of course, Ontario Hydro has adopted the nuclear energy route and has certainly shown how great the corporation can really be.
I am disappointed that no further income has come into AECL's treasury via royalties from these two companies. I would have to say to the Minister of Privatization that I hope he will sincerely support the Minister of Energy in this House, in Cabinet, to make sure that the parent corporation is funded and that that great research and development, of which we have seen the results over a period of 47 years since the founding of the AECL Corporation in 1952, be continued as a thriving operation and continue to produce companies and great works and world famous products for Canada.
December 12, 1989

In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate and thank the science community who, over the years, have contributed so much in the 45 years to research that has gone on in these two companies and the great work that it has done in combating one of the worst diseases we have in our society today, that being cancer. I would only encourage them to continue to do more.
I hope that the Minister of Energy, the Minister of State for Privatization, the Prime Minister and others will come to grips with the fact that this Crown corporation has got to continue. It has to be the parent company that is going to produce many more products and companies and be a great asset to Canada, not only for the revenue but for the social economic good of the entire country.

I think this small bill in fact raises some major issues. It is a bill which has not, as with many bills which go through the House of Commons, received a great deal of public attention. In fact, it is a bill which raises in quite a dramatic way a number of important points which are quite significant for the future of our country and, to some degree, the future of our parliamentary system.
The first question is whether active parts of the nuclear industry should be privatized. I suspect that most people across this country would share my sense of unease at the privatization of parts of the nuclear industry. The president of the union at Nordion who was speaking on behalf of his workers said:
On the issue of health and safety, the membership is concerned that under privatization the major concern of the new company would be high profit versus safety. The high cost of fail-proof safety systems might be more than the new company will be willing to install and maintain.
He went on to say:
It is our membership's belief that a government-owned establishment is more responsible to its employees' needs in health and safety.
As well, he said:
-a government-owned nuclear industry must be responsible to the public and respect the public's views of the unknown in the nuclear industry. A private company is only responsible to its shareholders and its customers.
Government Orders
That was Mr. Frank Amyot, the president of Local 70367 of the Public Service Alliance of Canada who is president of the largest group of employees of Nordion International. That is a person who represents workers in this company. Mr. Eades, president of Local 70367 of Theratronics, made the point that:
Given the choice, most employees would prefer to remain a Crown corporation because of the disruption to our pensions, possible changes in working conditions and the apprehension of whether the business is viable at the present time as a private company.
I think this may be simply a misguided sense of nuclear power within our society. But, part of it has to reflect the realities of recent years within our world such as the accident at Chernobyl which only recently we have come to understand was much greater in terms of the negative impact on people and the environment than we were given to understand at that time. So there is a concern across this country with respect to the nuclear industry.
I would have to say were I a government minister searching industries for firms to privatize, the privatization of the nuclear industry would not spring to mind as something that most Canadians would feel comfortable with and strongly support. I think most Canadians, if they look south to the United States, would receive some further support for their scepticism.
The nuclear industry in the United States is by and large in private hands and because of that has been an industry which has created serious fears right across the United States. My constituents live nine miles from a major United States nuclear plant which has been identified as one of the least reliable and one of the most mistake-ridden of any nuclear power plant in the United States.
My constituents ask, why is this the case? They have come to the conclusion that a big reason for the mistake is the pressure of powerful private sector individuals and corporations who are behind this particular power plant, Fermi II, who have pushed it ahead without sufficient attention to safety and the health, not just of workers in that plant, but to the safety and health of communities on the U.S. and Canadian sides of the border.
The previous Liberal member who spoke I think made a valid point when he stated that we have a different kind of nuclear technology in this country. It is a kind of nuclear technology which nevertheless leaves us with

December 12, 1989
Government Orders
tremendous waste products. We have not yet found a solution on how to get rid those waste products.
I believe, as someone who worries about the environmental future of our country, that it is simply inexcusable that we should continue to produce nuclear waste which we do not know how to get rid of, despite the fact that we have produced those nuclear wastes now for probably 30 to 40 years in this country.
I think there is a significant question which needs to be asked about whether it makes sense to privatize the nuclear industry. Most of us on this side of the House, certainly in the New Democratic Party, have very severe concerns about the privatization of two parts of the nuclear industry for the first time, and it is for that reason that we will not be able to support this privatization.
We also think, however, that there are some very important questions which need to be asked about the whole privatization thrust of this government. Much of it is a reflection of an ideological commitment, rather than the application of any kind of common sense, the application of an economic analysis, or an environmental analysis of what should be taking place in our country.
It seems to us that this is especially the case with respect to this particular set of privatizations. With Nordion and Theratronics, the minister and his officials have tried to paint for us a picture of these firms as somehow separate from the Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. It seems to me that in reality Nordion and Theratronics were in the past and continue to be very tightly integrated into AECL's operations. They depend on AECL for their nuclear material. In so far as they do not depend on AECL, they depend on Ontario Hydro which is yet another public enterprise in this country.
It seems to me that to artificially take these two enterprises and to privatize them when they are caught in an excess of public enterprises is simply to a make gesture for the sake of ideology, which makes no sense from any practical perspective. I could continue to talk about the principles which are involved with respect to privatizations. I think it is perhaps especially unfortunate that this government has never at any stage given us any
principles by which it intends to assess whether a company should or should not become privatized.
It seems to me that one must have some logical principles from which to begin before one can perceive and make sensible decisions with respect to privatization. I urge this government at some stage to make a statement with respect to its principles in thinking about privatization.
I am pleased that we have at least been able to maintain another important principle, the principle that high tech industries which Canadian taxpayers have paid to build in this country should have to remain in Canadian hands.
We have maintained the principle of Canadianization. With respect to Nordion it has been maintained at 25 per cent. In return for certain agreements on our side, the government has conceded that it would accept a constraint of 49 per cent with respect to Theratronics, so far as Canadian control is concerned.
I have to congratulate the government for accepting the need to listen occasionally to the opposition, and the need to see in this case the logic of applying Canadianization principles to both companies.
I have to finish with some final words of regret. I have been occupied elsewhere as some in the House have noted. I have to say in looking back over the committee proceedings at the legislative committee stage for this bill-and I know the minister shares my view with respect to this-there was a very vast and very sad effort on the part of the Conservative members of that committee to rush this bill through legislative committee.
Legislative committee, as members across this House have seen it, is a stage that permits members of the public to express their questions, concerns and uncertainties; to have them cleared up and in some cases accepted, and in other cases rejected. It is an important part of the new approach to the development and consideration of legislation which the House of Commons has adopted in recent years. I am therefore very disappointed that the legislative committee in this case did not even give consideration to the suggested witnesses from the opposition, neither from the Liberal party nor from ourselves in the New Democratic Party. I hope that this will never happen again in the future.
December 12, 1989

I would conclude on a non-partisan note by simply quoting one of the Conservative members of that committee, a member known to the speaker himself, the member from Edmonton-Strathcona. I think the whole House should take his words very seriously for the future. He said:
I would agree with the two opposition members. Having gone to all that work, as you have done, and having phoned those witnesses, it is unfair on our side not to have notified you. It is my understanding that the government would like this through, and that is why we are proceeding.
As a member of Parliament who sits on the Elections, Privileges, Procedures and Private Members' Business Committee, I think this does a great disservice to the process of legislative committees. I would just like to sympathize with you. I understand your concern.
I would hope in the future that we would see not just an understanding of the concern of the opposition that legislative committees operate successfully and fairly, but that these committees operate with a sense of fairness for everybody throughout this House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to speak again on Bill C-13, an act to authorize the divestiture of Nordion International Incorporated and Theratronics International Limited.
In the spirit of co-operation that the government through its minister has shown in addressing one major concern raised by the official opposition and the other opposition, that of safeguarding the majority control of shares by Canadians and thereby safeguarding the interests of Canadians, I would like to give credit to the government.
Speaking of credit, I would like to compliment my colleague for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke for his dutiful and careful study of the bill, for the detailed amendments placed on the Order Paper and for sensitizing the government to the need to guarantee majority Canadian ownership of these two companies and thereby use these companies properly as instruments of public policy.
A year ago in December when I entered Parliament I recall having said that Parliament is an institution not only for the government, but for the Canadian people. It is a forum for reconciliation of competing ideas. Today we have shown that the opposition truly has a significant and important role in our parliamentary system, if only
Government Orders
the government would from time to time and hopefully more frequently, listen to the opposition.
The bill, as amended, now allows the companies to be used as instruments of public policy. What do I mean by that? We will be able, by the continuing Canadian ownership of these companies, to use these companies as sources of revenues to finance and to allow jobs for Canadians; to ensure that research and development are undertaken on Canadian soil; to fund our many social programs such as medicare which is a program for all citizens; and to ensure the health and safety of Canadians, both consumers and employees.
Also Canadian ownership will allow us to set standards for health safety for other citizens of the world just as we do for Canadians. We will ensure that the availability of necessary nuclear technology for medical health, like cobalt therapy, will be ensured at reasonable cost and that last but not least, we will have the ability to impose environmental standards agreeable to the Canadian philosophy.
Speaking of philosophy, it should be a Canadian philosophy of approach insofar as nuclear technology and its development and use are concerned that we ought to always control it. It is so sensitive an area that we cannot let it go and pass to foreign hands.
In conclusion, the bill was amended by the government largely due I would say to the sensitization brought about by the opposition. I thank my colleague again. With the government having listened once at least, we will ensure a "Canadians first" policy. On behalf of Winnipeg North, my constituents in that riding, I welcome this amended bill and support it. Again, in the spirit of Christmas, I would like to see more of this happening for the interest of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, as you will know, by prior agreement we have decided to cut off the debate on this issue in about four minutes. I shall now proceed to give one of my famous short speeches. It may be my shortest speech of all. You may decide whether it is famous when I am finished, Mr. Speaker.
First I want to congratulate my friend for Renfrew- Nipissing-Pembroke. I tell the minister that I take pride in holding the record for another speech in another House.

December 12, 1989

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: I remember it.

That one, too. But in the Newfoundland House of Assembly it only went 16 hours and 42 minutes. The member is lucky we have a limit today. I congratulate my good friend for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke because he has done so much work on this bill and he has finally beaten some sense into the minister and the government.
I harken back to what my friend for Essex-Windsor was saying a minute ago about the committee process. I hope the government has learned another lesson. We have made the point during debate, and there is not time to make it at any length right now, but I believe members in the chamber know exactly what I am talking about. The government tried a particular ploy. It must admit that ploy is in disarray. Sending in the parliamentary goons to shut down the committee did not work. It worked in the short term because might is right in that situation. It had the numbers to shut down the committee.
Upon reflection, what we have done here in the last two or three days in the House could easily be done in an hour. The minister knows that and I know that. The reason it took several days is because we did not get an opportunity to do it in committee. We give notice again that we are going to have our say on those matters.
I would hope we can have our say in committee. I would also hope we can allow other people to come before the committee to have their say on matters of concern to them. But if the government keeps shutting us down in committee, we give notice we will take the time it requires to do it right here on the floor of the House.
We would rather it be in committee because that is where we can bring other people, people who are not elected members of the House but nevertheless have concerns about whether the nuclear industry ought to be privatized, concerns about food irradiation, concerns about nuclear medicine and I could go on. I make an appeal again that the committee process be respected by the government.
Finally, let me comment on the question of research and development. This debate has been very revealing in
that particular regard. The government figures have been very revealing.
I saw the Minister of State for Forestry here a little while ago. I remember when he was in opposition and I was on the government side, he eloquently stated that when the Tories came to power there would be a great increase in the amount of dollars devoted to R and D. Well, he ought to look at the figures today. He will find that people are realizing from coast to coast that this government has not put its money where its mouth is on research and development. More and more of our research is being conducted outside the country, and we are the losers in many respects.
There are many other things I would like to say, but my time is up. I thank you for your usual tolerance.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday amendments to the Income Tax Act dealing with tax assistance for retirement savings were tabled in the House of Commons. By increasing the limit on the amount of retirement savings eligible for tax assistance, these amendments are largely to the benefit of high income earners; those who can afford to take advantage of the increased limits and shelter a larger proportion of their income in RRSPs.

Mr. Speaker, the only answer the people of Canso want to hear is that their plant will stay open. My supplementary is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, who sets fish quotas and who ought to know that the plant closing in Canso will utterly destroy this community. Will the minister commit himself today to doing the only thing that can save the community of Canso and that is set aside a certain quantity of fish in his 1990 managen-ment plan for the port of Canso so that the plant can stay open? speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what we are dealing with here is an attempt to manage the resource which is diminishing in terms of certain stocks, to manage the fishery resource of Atlantic Canada on a sustainable economic basis.
It is a fact, as officials of National Sea and provincial governments of Atlantic Canada recognize, that we have overcapacity in the processing sector and the harvesting sector. We have a downturn of world demand and the

December 12, 1989

price for the fish. All of these factors are leading us to this current and very unfortunate situation.
When we establish quotas we do not assign them to specific plants, but I am personally looking at the possibility of the underutilized species, which amount to over 100,000 metric tons of special species, being made available to some communities such as Canso if they can come forward with a viable economic plan.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat my question. Will the Minister undertake to reserve a quantity of fish for the poor of Canso so that the Canso plant can stay open? That is what they want.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have said and have always said, as has been the policy of the government for many years, that we do not identify specific quotas with specific communities. The hon. member knows that. If we did when we have such overcapacity, all plants would be running at such a low production volume that they would be economically non-viable. That is why, while we regret these difficult decisions that have been made, we are going to devote every effort to assisting the rebuilding of the economies of these communities.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. As he will know, the European Community has once again thumbed its nose at Canada. Today it proposed fish catches for 1990 off Newfoundland which would be more than three times the quotas suggested and assigned by NAFO.
I ask the Prime Minister: Does he now accept the obvious, that his belated campaign, after sitting on the issue for four years, to educate the European Community has been a total flop?
Does he not agree that the time has come to stand up to the European Community, particularly Spain and Portugal? I want to ask him what steps he has in mind to stop the rape of our fish stocks while there is still some fish left to catch out there.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that this government has taken unprecedented steps to remove foreign fishing efforts from within the 200-mile economic zone and to bring various sanctions and forms of
international diplomatic and political pressure to bear upon the members of the European Community that seem to defend the unacceptable practices of two members, Spain and Portugal in particular, that have been fishing vastly in excess of these quotas.
As of coming to this House an hour ago, I was not advised that the EEC had embraced any quotas for 1990. In fact I have been advised that that information will not be forthcoming for another week.

Mr. Speaker, let me advise the minister of the following, and I read to him: "The European Community, fuelling a long running dispute with quotas with Canada overfishing off the coast of Newfoundland, proposed Tuesday quotas for 1990 more than three times higher than those suggested".
I say to the minister by way of supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, that these are the facts. I heard his answer. I respect his answer, but my point to him is that that is not working. All the minister has said has resulted in one big fat zero.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course we have achieved significant progress since 1986 when the level of foreign overfishing by these countries reached an all-time peak. We have seen that level of overfishing decrease persistently these past three years, but it is still vastly in excess of the quotas that the NAPO scientific panel has been recommending.
We will continue to work. We have appointed a special ambassador on marine conservation, Ambassador Alan Beesley, and ministers are working in all of the international fora, including the Prime Minister and other ministers of this government, to bring the appropriate pressure to bear and to point out that these are not practices consistent with good international conserva-tionism.

When those countries fish on the areas known as the nose and tail of the Grand Banks, beyond our 200-mile economic limit, we have to resort to various kinds of international pressure; sanctions such as the closures of

ports and representation in the various fora of the international community such as the OECD, Commonwealth and other fora.
The Prime Minister and members of this cabinet have taken such initiatives, including making such representation to members of the community of nations and we will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the right hon. Prime Minister. It concerns the incident yesterday in which Her Majesty's Canadian destroyer Saguenay, on patrol off George's Bank, was repeatedly and aggressively rammed by a U.S. scallop dragger, the Concordia, out of New Bedford, Massachusetts, after being ordered to stop for inspection for fishing illegally in Canadian waters.
In view of the overwhelming difficulties our country, and Atlantic Canada in particular, is experiencing due to overfishing and the grave national concern this is causing right now as indicated by the questions we have just heard, particularly from the Member for Cape Breton- Highlands-Canso, can the Prime Minister say what positive action has been taken by the Canadian government in response to this incident?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the incident that the hon. member refers to was caused by the need for the use of ship days by the Department of National Defence for the Department of Fisheries to provide fisheries surveillance to that department.
As the hon. member knows well, probably better than anyone in this House, there are rules of engagement. It is not the practice of the Canadian navy to jeopardize civilian lives. Every effort was made in this instance to have the scallop trawler turn around. The opportunities were given to the trawler by American coast guard officials who recommended that they surrender. The actions that were taken by the captain, on directions, were appropriate but at no time, and I am sure the hon. member would agree, should HMCS Saguenay have risked the lives of those men on that ship who indeed were breaking Canadian law.
The difficulty, as he knows, is to use force without causing the loss of life to civilians and that is the appropriate action that was taken yesterday.

I thank the hon. minister for his answer to my question and, yes, I am very familiar with the rules for engagement. In fact, I have had to use them occasionally.
The name of the game with rules for engagement is minimum force required to do what it is you have to do. I would remind the House of an action taken by HMCS Athabaskan in 1985 when two Spanish vessels were arrested by armed boarding parties that were sent on board. A Canadian crew was put on board and they were towed back to St. John's, Newfoundland in Canadian waters.
Hear, hear!

It is very obvious that Saguenay was in hot pursuit of the Concordia, and by that I mean she was detected in Canadian waters and followed outside into international waters. On the basis that HMCS Saguenay has a top speed of 28 knots, why could our warship not overtake-which she could do-this particular vessel, stop it, board it, arrest it and take it back to Canadian waters and charge it, and not let it return to home port where it was going to get a much smaller penalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague has pointed out that the rules of engagement involving violations of Canada's fishing laws also require a degree of prudence in terms of the forms of escalation that are used in these matters.
I might tell the House that had we the co-operation of the opposition parties so that our patrol vessels could be used to their full capacity by the return of fisheries patrol vessels and others to service, we might not have this kind of problem today.
Oh, oh.

Oh, oh.

Was it signed "Love, Brian"?

December 12, 1989

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans

Mr. Speaker, as a result of the onset of dusk last evening, it was not possible to continue the pursuit with a view to boarding, in dangerous conditions, this vessel. Today, officials of External Affairs have again met with officials of the U.S. embassy to ensure and secure the co-operation of U.S. authorities in this matter. The U.S. Ambassador has given his personal commitment to co-operate and ensure that such measures are taken.

statistics for 1988. It showed that the proportion of poor persons in Canada fell to 13.1 per cent in 1988 from 14.1 in 1987. Since 1984, almost 760,000 persons have escaped poverty.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, considering the finance minister's comments yesterday about the lack of agreement on the finance committee, I would like to ask him the following question. Mr. Speaker, I understand the concern that the hon. member is expressing about the level of interest rates in this country. It is something that has been expressed on a number of occasions.
As I said as recently as yesterday in the House, certainly last week, we do have some very real concerns about elements of the inflationary pressures that are in our economy. I think it is very important that we get these out of the economy as quickly as we can. Once we have been able to do that we can see lower rates. Until we get confidence up and we have dealt with the inflation problem once and for all, I think it would be wrong to move precipitously.
I just draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that in the late 1970s governments did ignore the inflation problem and that led us to the mess of 1981-82, and I am sure the hon. member does not want to repeat that.

be introduced at 7 per cent has not really changed Canadians' minds about this tax grab.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. It has long been a fundamental principle of our parliamentary system that all government revenues are received in a consolidated manner and are not designated for specific purposes except through the annual budgetary process.
Recently we have seen some modest departures from this principle. For example, in the plant breeders' rights legislation certain royalties have been redirected for specific plant research, and in New Brunswick the provincial government has imposed a new fuel tax which is directly dedicated to highway construction.
In our environment committee, Mr. Speaker, we have had several proposals recently for a so-called carbon tax to provide funds for environmental research on atmospheric pollution or, as some would urge, to be used for Trans-Canada Highway improvements.

Is the government willing to reconsider the principles of revenue consolidation for dedicated funding purposes or user fee concepts? If not, are there other effective existing ways to direct government revenues from specific sources to specific purposes?

Mr. Speaker, the government has, over the last few years, been dedicating quite a bit of effort to user fee concepts so that people who are using a service of the government are asked to pay for that fee through some form of user fee or other charge.
Moving from there to the broader concept of what the hon. member has asked about, whether there can be dedicated taxes, these are a good deal more complex and more difficult to achieve. It is something that I have not a closed mind on by any means, but I would caution him that there are difficulties in doing so and in recent years governments have been trying to move away from this type of approach rather than moving toward it in a broader sense. This is something on which, as I said, we have an open mind on.

speechtext:

to serve a Parliament anywhere in the industrialized world.
What we are trying to do is to further improve the conditions under which public servants function, their remuneration, their incentives to be better, more skilled managers, and to be able to exercise within their spheres of managerial responsibility greater personal leadership.
