speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have already heard a description of Bill C-23 and its objectives. I would like to outline the consideration which guided the government to introduce certain amendments.
The committee of this House which examined the bill heard numerous and very competent witnesses. The government has paid heed to the substantive concerns those witnesses raised. Our amendments responded to those concerns. But I would like to point out that the amendments are consistent with the policy announced by the minister last fall.
In the original version of the bill, if the Governor in Council designated an application for a full review by the

National Energy Board, it would specify issues to be examined during the review. In other words, the Governor in Council would say to the board, "Along with whatever else you deem to be relevant, be sure you examine these areas." This measure was intended simply to let applicants and interested parties know why an application was being designated for public hearings.
However, some utilities which appeared before the committee had reservations. They were concerned that this provision could result in arbitrary criteria being imposed upon a particular applicant. In light of these comments, we have removed the provisions allowing the Governor in Council to specify concerns about an individual application.
The original bill provided that if the board approved a proposal without hearings, the Governor in Council, within six months, could order a review which would include hearings. Witnesses before the committee said six months is too long to delay an export or the start of construction of an international power line. The very publicly visible process entailed in this bill gives interested parties ample time and opportunity to formulate and submit their views before the board makes a decision. Therefore, should a difficulty arise after a board decision, it will come to the attention of the minister and the Governor in Council in short order. The government has reduced the time period in question to 45 days.
I would also like to comment upon the submission to the committee by the Grand Council of the Crees of Quebec. The Cree are concerned that there be a thorough public review process for proposed hydroelectric developments in northern Quebec. Should such developments entail exports, an assessment of the environmental impacts of the export proposal must be submitted with the National Energy Board application. Further, interested parties may submit their views to the board. If the board has reason to believe that there has not been a thorough and adequate environmental assessment, its duty is clear. It recommends public hearings.
However, I am pleased to point out that steps have already been taken to ensure that new hydro developments in northern Quebec receive thorough scrutiny. Our colleague, the Minister of the Environment, presently is engaged in discussions with his Quebec counterpart to establish a joint federal-provincial process of public review. The Cree and Inuit will have a major role
Government Orders
to play in the review process. They have already been invited to assist the government in planning and setting up the review process and will participate in the review itself.
Some hon. members have expressed other reservations about this bill. These are matters to which the government has given consideration and which, upon reflection, we believe to be unfounded. Let me discuss them briefly.
Some claim that the existing National Energy Board Act is just fine as it is. Well, in 1986, the NEB held a public inquiry into the regulation of electricity exports. During that inquiry, representatives of many utilities, provincial government officials and other interested parties complained of the duplication between provincial and federal review processes.
Let me illustrate the impact that this duplication of regulatory procedures can have. An Alberta utility, which recently appeared before the legislative committee, said it would be reluctant to propose to build an international power line. It said that the regulatory burden would be too great. The utility also pointed out that the lives of those living or owning land along the proposed power line corridor would be disrupted throughout the whole provincial and then federal regulatory processes. Our policy eliminates needless duplication, while ensuring Canadian interests are safeguarded.
The NEB act also needed to be updated with a new listing of key criteria the board should consider in reviewing an electricity application. Bill C-23 makes environmental protection a priority. It also ensures Canadians will be given the opportunity of fair access to electricity supplies before those supplies are committed to export.
Some have criticized this bill because it gives the final say as to whether an application will be subject to federal public hearings to the Governor in Council. These critics argue we should retain the procedure in the existing National Energy Board Act, or leave it to the National Energy Board to decide whether hearings will be heard.
I, and other speakers, have explained the need to amend the existing act, so as to avoid duplicating provincial reviews of an application. Clearly, if unwarranted duplication of good work at the provincial level is to be avoided, some discretion must be employed in determining when hearings at the federal level are

December 12, 1989
Government Orders
required. The question is: How do we establish sound processes to govern the use of this discretion?
We have heard many views on this matter. We have heard that you cannot leave these decisions entirely with the board. It has been argued that if a regulatory agency is placed in the position of repeatedly having to decide the degree of regulation to apply to proposals, the agency will tend to over-regulate.
Conversely, some have argued that if the Governor in Council alone ruled upon what review should take place, it would tend to avoid public hearings. Others have said cabinet might have a bias in favour of holding hearings.
The procedure set out in Bill C-23 involves both the board and the Governor in Council in the decision process. It establishes checks and balances between them to ensure that sound decisions are made about the extent of federal review.
The role of the board is to make a recommendation to the Governor in Council based upon its assessment of an application and the review of that application conducted at the provincial level. The National Energy Board will examine views submitted by interested parties and whatever considerations the board itself deems relevant. The check on the board is the fact that it must back up its recommendation by publicly stating the reasons it believes hearings are warranted and those reasons must be sufficient to guide the Governor in Council.
I would point out that the process for dealing with an application for an electricity export or an international power line takes place in the full light of public scrutiny. Applications, supporting documentation, the board's decisions and the reasons for those decisions all will be available to the public. And there will be plenty of opportunity for interested parties to comment to the board before it decides whether to recommend hearings.
The role of the Governor in Council in this process is to review the National Energy Board's recommendation and to decide whether to designate an application for hearings. It is obvious that a recommendation from such a respected agency as the National Energy Board, made in such a highly public fashion, will carry great weight with the Governor in Council. That is confirmed by histoiy. Governor in Council authority over the National Energy Board recommendations is nothing new. Since the board was created 30 years ago, the approval of the Governor in Council has been required for all major
board decisions respecting oil, natural gas and electricity exports. In all that time-three decades-not once has the Governor in Council overturned an export recommendation from the board. There is no reason to believe that trend will change.
Mr. Speaker, the government found the legislative committee's work on this bill valuable. We paid close attention to these deliberations, reflected upon them and acted upon some of the concerns raised. I would like to express my sincere thanks to everybody who participated, both with speeches in the House and with work in the legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, we have come to the third reading stage of Bill C-23 where we debate the legislation in its final form.
I would like to explain this afternoon why I feel Bill C-23 should not be passed. There are two main reasons for this. One is that the bill does not adhere to the principle behind the bill as stated by the government. The other reason is that, as I said yesterday, I strongly disagree with what Bill C-23 in fact does. It takes the
December 12, 1989

power from the National Energy Board and gives it to the cabinet.
Under Bill C-23 the cabinet will make the final decision as to whether there is a public inquiry on applications of electricity exports and power lines.
First let us deal with how the bill contradicts the stated intention of the government. During the second reading of Bill C-23, the deputy House leader twice referred to the principle behind Bill C-23. On one occasion the deputy House leader said that the basic principle governing the new policies was that there should be no unwarranted duplication of federal and provincial regulation. "Elsewhere" he said "the National Energy Board should complement and not duplicate measures taken by provincial governments". That is the basic principle underlying the amendments contained in this bill.
The deputy House leader in his speech referred to the history that led up to Bill C-23. He mentioned how provincial regulation of electricity is much greater today than it was 30 years ago when the National Energy Board was formed and therefore why a second layer of federal regulation was no longer necessary.
That is fine. I am familiar with the provisions of Bill C-23 which accomplish these objectives, but the source of the problem is not so much in the government's desire to reduce regulations but in its desire for more power over electricity trade. It is this second motive that I think will do the most harm and which I believe could in some cases result in increased regulation of electricity.
If I can be blunt, we are setting the stage for out and out political interference by the cabinet in the electricity business. As I argued yesterday, this bill gives the federal cabinet new powers to stop a federal hearing on an electricity power line or an export application to the National Energy Board.
As we know, the present situation is if an application comes before the board for electricity export or an application for an international power line, there is a public inquiry. However, under Bill C-23 the National Energy Board will issue a permit or, if it thinks there
Government Orders
should be a hearing, it will recommend to cabinet that there be a hearing; but cabinet must have the final say.
Under this measure the federal government will be able to speed up an application through the board or, more important, shield it from public spotlight.
That kind of meddling has not been acceptable for the past 30 years ever since the National Energy Board started, and it is certainly not acceptable today. Not only is it unacceptable; it runs contrary to the stated principle behind Bill C-23.
Nowhere in the speech of the deputy House leader, or in any of the departmental policy documents is there a reason stated for giving this kind of power to the federal cabinet. The only explanation came from the minister himself in response to a question that I put to him at a legislative committee. When asked why the board was not given the power to make the call on whether there should be a public inquiry, the minister gave a farfetched explanation of why the NEB would be in an apparent conflict of interest situation.
As reported in the Minutes and Evidence of Proceedings of the legislative committee on Bill C-23 the minister stated:
There is the perception that the board would be in a conflict of
interest situation, because the board would literally be deciding how
much more work it makes for itself.
That argument is totally false, as I explained to the House yesterday. Not only is the reason false; it seems that it was something that the minister said on the spur of the moment during the committee meeting. That argument certainly does not appear anywhere in the department's documents concerning Bill C-23.
Did the department forget to mention the reason for the single most important change heralded in this Bill C-23? No, I think not. I think the answer the minister gave represents the true principle, or it is the true principle behind the bill showing through, that is, that Bill C-23 is designated to give more power to cabinet over electricity applications to the National Energy Board.
There was an article in The Calgary Herald this week which seemed to indicate that this policy would spill over into oil and gas export applications as well. The government is apparently thinking of preventing the board from holding hearings on any export applications that it deems too sensitive. Not only would that make a mockery of the

December 12, 1989
Government Orders
National Energy Board, it would result in an energy policy that suits the government's political instincts and interests rather than this country's long-term interests. It is the same political principle behind Bill C-23.
Bill C-23 is not a technical document. It is a political document that the government is trying to pass for a technical one. It may very well pass, but let there be no doubt about what we are debating and giving third reading. It is really a licence for political interference.
I conclude my remarks and recommend, for the above reasons and for the reasons which I stated yesterday during debate on this bill, that the House not pass Bill C-23.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to repeat all the arguments we have already made on this bill during second reading debate last June and again in greater detail during meetings of the legislative committee in November. However, I do think the major points bear reiteration.
The first major point I would like to reiterate is that this bill is not about energy regulation. It is about energy exports. It is about a continental market for Canadian generated electricity. That is the principle at the heart of the bill. This entire shuck and jive about regulation is just that. It is a smoke screen and ought not to be allowed to get in the eyes of the prudent and sensible members of this House. However, more on that a bit later.
I would like, at first, if I may, to construct a little context here. The previous Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stated in his speech to the board of directors of the Canadian Electrical Association on November 26, 1987: "Electricity's importance cannot be overestimated''. He was quite right. The National Energy Board went even further in its report on the regulation of electricity exports, which was released in 1987, stating that in most uses "electricity qualifies as an essential commodity". A most trenchant assessment. There is every reason to believe that electricity will become even more important in the future. It will come to be considered a strategic resource.
The United States, Canada and other countries are becoming increasingly concerned about global warming which is caused in large part by the burning of fossil fuels, and there is no question that electricity has associated with it a host of environmental problems.
These include, for example, in the case of hydroelectric facilities, the flooding of valleys and the destruction of the way of life of indigenous peoples. In the case of nuclear power, there is the never-ending problem of nuclear waste. In the case of natural gas-fired and especially coal-fired generating stations, there is acid rain and carbon dioxide emissions which contribute to global warming.
We in the New Democratic Party firmly believe that all of these environmental problems mean that how we produce electricity-and, even more important, how we conserve it-will become increasingly important in the future. The fact remains that electricity is convenient. There is also a widespread perception that electricity is clean. This reputation is mainly due to the fact that electricity is clean where it is used. In general, most of the environmental problems are associated with generating it, not with using it. But that perception of the cleanliness of electricity exists, and it means that the demand in the United States for electricity generated in Canada is bound to increase.
What has this government done in response to this new reality? Has it made changes to protect, to safeguard this strategic resource? Has the government added extra protections for our energy security just to be on the safe side, to be prudent? It is just the opposite. This government is making it easier to export electricity to the United States, and it is doing so immediately after it signed a deal that threatens our future energy security by assuring our United States customers a never decreasing supply of our strategic energy resources.
This government signed a free trade deal with the U.S. that will act like ratchet on our energy supplies. The proportionality clause, as it is known, will be, as was so trenchantly observed by my seat mate, the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley yesterday, a boa constrictor around the neck of our energy security. From now on, every single proposal to build a power line or to export electricity takes on a degree of importance that just was not there before. And I say every single proposal, including those for export of the so-called interruptibles because the interruptibles too-as the minister finally admitted in the committee after I perhaps unkindly badgered him for several minutes and several questions-are included in the total energy
December 12, 1989

exports noted in the free trade agreement as being subject to the proportionality ratchet.
Every new kilowatt hour of exported electricity will, in effect, set the floor for Canadian offers to export electricity in the future. It seems inevitable that the export of this strategic resource will be jacked up and up and up over the years. In the face of this situation where every export proposal essentially circumscribes our energy future, where every export proposal sets the limit on our future .energy flexibility, this government in this bill is making public hearings on these export proposals less frequent. Indeed it is making them optional. That is right, Mr. Speaker-optional.
There will be no requirement for a public hearing on export proposals. There will be no requirement for a public hearing on the building of export transmission lines. The decision will be, in the first instance, up to whatever provincial regulatory authority may seize the power conferred on it by this bill, and in the second instance, by the National Energy Board, always subject to the cabinet saying: "Sorry, NEB, you are off base, they can go ahead without a hearing". For all but exceptional cases, exports will be approved by the NEB without a public hearing.
In those cases where the NEB believes that a public hearing is warranted, for example, in the case of a proposal to export a huge amount of hydroelectricity, this bill gives the cabinet the power to block that public hearing, and even when a public hearing is held there is no provision for reasonable intervener funding for those wishing to bring absolutely pertinent information to the attention of the body holding that public hearing.
Not only is that imprudent; it is dangerous, it is foolish, it is totally unacceptable, which is why in the committee I attempted to propose amendments that would at least guarantee that in the event of the construction of a hydroelectric export power line, or in the event of an application for the export of electricity, somebody at the provincial or the federal level, it does not matter, somebody would hold a public hearing. The government members defeated that amendment and leave us consequently with the bill before us today.
Government Orders
In an attempt to justify this bill, the government has claimed that the electricity industry is over-regulated: in the aspects of the construction of interprovincial power lines and export power lines, and in the event of electricity exported south as a commodity, there is over-regulation to a degree that must be dealt with because apparently the industry is suffering accordingly.
What are the facts, Mr. Speaker? The National Energy Board has never refused an electricity export application. Not once. Never. Is this over-regulation? This is an export holiday.
During the legislative committee hearings, no one- and I asked them all: not the minister, not the chairman of the NEB, not a single witness-could come up with an example where they or any person in the industry was harmed by this alleged over-regulation. Not one instance. Only one witness was able to point to a case where inappropriate regulation had the effect of discouraging a project, and that was in my own province.
TransAlta Utilities said that because of the current regulatory environment they would not even bother applying to build a line across British Columbia because B.C. Hydro would stomp all over them. Fine. But that is an instance not of over-regulation, rather it is an instance of inappropriate regulation. Not duplication, not excessive regulation, but inappropriate regulation. And that we have no objection to dealing with. But that is not what this bill does.
This bill, rather, eradicates the final effective control of the National Energy Board, in the public interest, to oversee the prudent husbanding of electricity in the national interest in Canada.
We agree changes to existing legislation need to be made, especially in light of the disastrous free trade agreement. But the changes should not reduce the safeguards on our energy future. They should add a greater degree of protection for our strategic-dare I mention it-Canadian energy resources.
By way of conclusion, let me highlight one last item which I think illustrates clearly the direction in which this government is headed. There was a time-there really was-when the Conservative party believed that Canadians should benefit most from our resources, that

December 12, 1989
Speaker's Ruling
most of the benefit of our natural advantages should not go to our neighbours and business competitors to the south in the United States, but should go to Canadians.
Listen to what the then Prime Minister said back in 1959. You may even remember this personally, Mr. Speaker. Let me quote from Hansard at page 4025, from a speech given in this House on May 26, 1959, by the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker:
-no longer will there be any suspicion that the Canadian consumer is being forced to subsidize the foreign markets or that Canadian industries will be asked to pay higher prices for their energy than those paid by foreign industries using Canadian energy.
The Mulroney Conservatives are selling out the Diefenbaker principles. Many Canadians know that the free trade agreement prevents our government from ever guaranteeing that Canadians will pay significantly less than American customers for our own energy resources, including electricity generated in Canada.
But what many Canadians do not yet know is that the Mulroney Conservatives will apply their new super tax, be it at 9 per cent or 7 per cent, to energy sold in Canada, but they will not apply it to energy sold to the United States. This means that Canadians could end up paying consistently more for Canadian energy resources.
Might I ask when is a natural advantage not a natural advantage? When it is left to the tender mercies of so blind and heedless a government. And what a government it is. Under the Conservative doubly whammy of the free trade deal and the GST, Canadian energy consumers will be penalized for living in Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, we should be husbanding our strategic energy resources jealously. We should conduct open, public hearings when deciding whether to export electricity. We should protect the independence of the chief regulatory body, the National Energy Board. We should ensure that Canadians, not Americans, gain the most from our own Canadian energy resources. But, the government, in each instance, principally in this bill, is legislating the opposite.
This bill, even at this late date should be defeated, soundly defeated.

Motion No. 1.
That Bill C-12 be amended in Clause 9 by adding immediately
after line 17 at page 6 the following:
"(2) Notwithstanding sub-section (1) the Canadian Museum of Civilization may not sell, exchange, give away, destroy or otherwise dispose of any native artifacts without written consent of the native community from which it originated."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think it is in the interests of the House and those interested in this bill that we do what we can to deal with the various issues promptly so that possibly we can deal with this by five o'clock. I would be even more encouraged in that resolve if I heard
December 12, 1989

sounds of enthusiasm from the government for these very good amendments that my Liberal colleague and I have put forward. We will see how the discussion goes.
Let me address specifically Motion No. 1. The motion proposes that there be a restriction on the right of the Canadian Museum of Civilization in respect of the disposition of native artefacts and that the restriction be that those artefacts could not be disposed of without the written consent of the native community from which they originated.
The underlying point behind this amendment is an acknowledgement that the House must make as to the treatment of native artefacts over the last 100 years. In many, many native communities across this country, the non-native community, the Government of Canada, private citizens, church groups and others have treated native artefacts as not the property and heritage of native people in the communities from which they have come but, instead, as something which could just take from them. That is not only a deep injustice. It is clearly a grievance of the native community in this country.
We had witnesses before the committee from the Kamloops area who discussed these issues and had a number of proposals to put to us. At one stage I put an amendment to the committee that would have representatives of the native communities serve on the various boards that are being established under this legislation.
Regretfully, Liberals and government members voted against it. I hope, as days pass, that they will find a way to recant from that particular position. I would hope the government, in making its appointments, will consult with the native leadership in this country to see if it can find its way to appoint representatives of the native community to these particular boards. It is important that we acknowledge the historic role of native people in the development of the treasures, the art treasures and historic treasures of this country.
I would urge upon the House that, at least as a minimum, we require the Canadian Museum of Civilization to seek and obtain the written consent of the native communities when it proposes to dispose of artefacts in its possession. This is an important issue of the native community, and one that I would hope would have the full support of this House.

The exception refers to those very few cases where the provenance of an artefact is unknown. In those rare cases, consent is not secured simply because the artefact has no identity with a known community.
There are numbers of examples of native artefacts from the Canadian Museum of Civilization which have now been devolved to museums and locations, many of them in the hon. member's province: 'Ksan Indian Village and Museum in Hazelton, the Umista Cultural Centre in Alert Bay, the Kwakkuit Museum at Cape Mudge, as well as the Thunder Bay Art Gallery and the Native Museum at Gleichen, Alberta.

Much of that collection will be going to the Northwest Territories. Indeed, the museum has the curator in residence program and curator training programs for curators from native and other museums.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. colleague for Victoria. The point was well made, and I think the sensitivity of the museology community and the boards of directors have been alerted by the hon. member bringing this to our attention at this time.
Debating it in committee is not as widespread as debating it within this House. I am sure that the interesting and legitimate concerns will now be far more carefully reviewed. She said: Mr. Speaker, in debating this bill on museums, I bring this particular amendment to the attention of the government because I consider that we are dealing with a very sensitive issue when it concerns Canadian cultural properties and Canadian cultural concerns.
It is my firm belief that Canadians have the talent, capacity and ability to fulfil the management positions, manage the funds, enable appropriate acquisitions, apply the mission statement or the mandate of the museum and be very creative in their approach to their responsibilities in the management of the four museums that we are referring to in this particular bill.
There is nothing more important than the historical record of Canada for Canadians, by Canadians and for the visitors to Canada. Our aboriginal people are our first founding peoples. Our bilingual nature is the result of our two founding European families who came from those nations which helped build this country. Our multicultural dimension is an increasingly important aspect of our Canadian reality which encompasses all our cultures. It is key that all of these realities be reflected in the board of directors and that they be Canadians of Canadian commitment and fulfil the roles that have been defined in this particular Bill.
I think that we have greatness in all walks of life in Canada and we can find the proper people to fill those jobs. I see no reason to have to look beyond our own
December 12, 1989

Canadian citizens in any way to fulfil the particular mandate that we have in mind.
There has been some concern expressed. While I understand that concern, I do not find it particularly well founded that those people who have chosen to come to live here in Canada but have not taken Canadian citizenship perhaps might not be enabled to sit on the boards of these four Canadian national museums.
To my knowledge, Canadian citizenship is required under the Constitution of Canada if we wish to be a member of this House of Commons. If you wish to summon someone to the Senate that person must be a Canadian citizen as well as a resident in the particular province that person is representing. If you wish to participate in the elections in Canada under the Canada Elections Act, you must be a citizen of Canada.
I suggest that there is no substantive jurisprudence and no clear precedent established that would indicate that we could not apply Section 1 of our Canadian Charter to say that it is reasonable and justifiable in an open and democratic society to have Canadian citizens, be they aboriginal, francophone, anglophone or from any one of our multicultural communities, represent the various required skills that enable a museum board to function most effectively.
I believe that we should and can have the kinds of expertise that we need to go out and market, explain and show the world the Canadian acquisitions that we have. I ask for the acceptance of Motion No. 2, hopefully with the understanding of the reasons behind this amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the concern that has been expressed about this particular motion, which I grant is on the side of the angels, is that it might infringe on the Charter, specifically the provisions of Section 15, the equality provisions.
In a recent decision in British Columbia the Supreme Court of Canada in the Law Society of British Columbia .v. Andrews et al, the finding was that a provision which restricted the right to practise law to Canadian citizens infringed upon the equality provisions of Section 15 of the Charter. There were two aspects to the analysis that was carried out.
Speaker's Ruling
To override a Charter-guaranteed right, the objective underlying the law must relate to concerns which are pressing and substantial in a free and democratic society. The nature and purpose of the enactment must be examined to decide whether the limitation represents a legitimate exercise to attain a desirable social objective which would warrant overriding constitutionally protected rights.
As a second stage of the analysis, a balancing of factors must take place, such as the nature and importance of the right of the individual or group concerned, the extent of its infringement, the degree to which the limitation furthers the attainment of the desired goal embodied in the legislation, and the broader social impact of both the impugned law and its alternatives.
All that having been said, there are some practical considerations too. I believe that the language which the hon. member has taken for her motion is parallel to the language that is in Bill C-40 which is also before this House. That bill is designed to protect the Canadian nature of our broadcasting system against all kinds of assailing forces which I need not go into here.
In this case, we are dealing with Canadian institutions, which are composed of Canadian exhibits by and large. All this having been said, Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to ask whether there would be consent of the House, and I ask the hon. member whether she would be disposed, to just drop the last six words of her motion. The words are "who is ordinarily resident in Canada". That would have the effect of admitting only Canadian citizens to the board but would remove the practical consideration and the practical worry of distinguished Canadians who, for reasons of health or other reasons, have found it necessary to live outside the country for periods of time. The words "ordinarily resident in Canada" might be an arguable proposition. To remove any doubt, would the hon. member be prepared to delete those last six words of her motion, and would there be the consent of the House?

Mr. Speaker, in response to the parliamentary secretary, I thank him for that consideration and I certainly would accept the removal of those last four words.
