The House resumed from Thursday, October 26, [DOT] consideration of the motion of Ms. Langan:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of negotiating with the provinces to provide a comprehensive Bill of Rights for children which would standardize laws throughout the country, and that this Bill of Rights include a child protection commission and an emergency hotline which children could contact in times of crisis.

Mr. Speaker, before I start my speech, perhaps I may recall that I had already started to speak to this motion on September 25,

Private Members' Business
and at the next opportunity, I was unfortunately, or fortunately, as you prefer, in Europe, which means that according to the Standing Orders, I still have ten minutes' speaking time.
Mr. Speaker, we welcome this opportunity to speak to the issue of children's rights, an opportunity afforded by the motion presented by the hon. member for Mission- Coquitlam (Ms. Langan).
This motion concerns the very important question of how we can guarantee and protect children's rights in Canada. We believe that children form the cornerstone of our society and the family, our most important institution. That is why any attempt to improve the living conditions of families and their members deserves our undivided attention as decision makers. This government recognizes the importance of protecting the basic rights of children and the need for helping families which have the primary responsibility for bringing up children.
On November 20, the United Nations adopted its Convention on the Rights of the Child. As you know, Canada played an active role in drafting the text of the convention, following efforts by both federal and provincial governments. In 1981, a federal-provincial task force was created to determine what the convention should contain, from a Canadian perspective. Several versions drafted by Canada were used as the basis for the convention itself.
The draft Convention on the Rights of the Child, proposed by the United Nations, is aimed at establishing an international standard. Its purpose is also to protect a variety of childrens' rights whether they are social, economic, political, religious or civil. The 54 draft articles guarantee the protection for children who have no family or who are exposed to abuse, and the right to social security.
This draft convention reflects a comprehensive view of childrens' rights and is international in scope. The countries that signed the convention will be monitored to ensure that progress is made on children's rights. For instance, two years after the convention is adopted, every signatory country will be asked to submit a report on the nature of the measures it has taken to promote the rights of the child.
The draft convention also provides for establishing an international panel of experts that will be responsible for evaluating the living conditions of children in the signatory countries.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, signing the international convention means that the laws of that country must conform to the provisions of the convention.
Several aspects of the international Convention on the Rights of the Child are a matter of provincial jurisdiction in this country, or that jurisdiction may be shared by provincial and federal authorities. As a result, the process of ratifying the United Nations Convention requires, in the Canadian context, the co-operation of both federal and provincial governments in order to consider very carefully the implications of this document for our existing policy and future action.
It is expected that a certain amount of harmonization will be necessary among the various Canadian provisions in order to meet the requirements of the convention. We should also remember that the Canadian government has taken a number of initiatives whose objectives have already been to promote the well-being and protection, and to guarantee the rights, of children in Canada. Such programs are also designed to help families and children experiencing difficult situations or major changes.
However, although we are better acquainted with the specific problems of Canadian families, we must not forget that most of these families, whatever their structure, take care of their members and are proud of their progress and success.
My point is that government assistance in protecting the rights of children should be complementary to the role played by families, not a substitute. Nevertheless, there are a number of very serious situations where families are unable to play that role satisfactorily.
The Minister of National Health and Social Welfare already followed up on part of the motion presented in the House, when he recently announced financing totalling $1.3 million for an emergency telephone service to be used by children in a crisis. I am referring to the "Kids Help Line". This free service offers immediate help to children across Canada, providing information appropriate to the situation and directing them to agencies that

December 12, 1989
Private Members' Business
may be able to provide longer term solutions for their problems.
In the mid 1980s, the Family Violence Prevention Division was created within the Department of National Health and Welfare to co-ordinate federal activities against family violence. The Division has a national information centre on family violence to inform the public and make it aware of this crucial issue.
In 1986, the government launched a five year $25-million initiative to fight the sexual abuse of children. This initiative includes legislation to amend the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act and measures to prevent sexual abuse of children and for protection and treatment.
In 1988, the government allocated $40 million to a four-year national family violence prevention initiative intended to create spaces in shelters for victims of family violence. Canada is not free of child poverty. That is why the federal government protects the most disadvantaged, including families with children, through the Canada Assistance Plan. Under this plan, the federal government shares the expenses incurred by the provinces for social assistance and some social services.
This year alone, the federal government plans to give the provinces over $5 billion under the plan. Nevertheless, there are encouraging signs in the battle against child poverty. Official statistics show that the number of poor children has decreased since 1984. The rapid rise in the number of families where both parents work outside the home and the increased number of single-parent families show us the importance of establishing an effective child care program. The federal government is already contributing to child care through the Canada Assistance Plan. We plan to spend $240 million this year to create more subsidized child care spaces.
Created in 1988 with a total budget of $100 million over a seven-year period, the Child Care Initiatives Fund is used to finance innovative child care projects to meet the special and diversified needs of children.
As announced by the Prime Minister and in the Speech from the Throne, a new national day care program will be implemented towards the end of this
Parliament. In terms of additional measures to maintain the economic standing of families, I would point to the child benefit system which includes, among other things, family allowances and child tax credits.
With the advent of the new Goods and Services Tax, the tax system will become more progressive and more equitable through a number of changes which will enable low income Canadians to apply for fiscal assistance. This is why families earning less than $30,000 a year will be in a better position once the GST is in force.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, all the activities, initiatives and programs we have just mentioned are only a few examples which show that the Canadian government is committed to protect the security rights of Canadian children and to help families.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this particular motion. I am going to read it because it is a very specific request to the government. It reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of negotiating with the provinces to provide a comprehensive Bill of Rights for children which would standardize laws throughout the country, and that this Bill of Rights include a child protection commission and an emergency hotline which children could contact in times of crisis.
Hotlines are not particularly unknown in this country and in the few cases where hotlines have been used for children, the use has been fairly extensive.
Today, I want to spend a little time on the intent of this motion. During the two-hour debate that has gone on, our party has put on record some of the considerations that we think are important in establishing an atmosphere for the raising of children and ensuring that those children are protected in all kinds of circumstances.
Canada is a country without equal when it comes to the social standards and social justice system that we have put in place. Canada has been a leading nation speaking out for human rights, speaking out for dignity of the person, on behalf of the kind of government which allows this kind of dignity and these kinds of human rights. It is the kind of democracy that recognizes the value of the individual.

We in Canada have seldom been found wanting when it comes to speaking out about the protection of the world's children. We have seldom been found wanting compared to other countries in the effort that we have made to make it possible for world's children to be a little better off than they would without our efforts. Those efforts have not necessarily been government efforts, but they have been the efforts of the individuals and families across Canada who see the possibility of harm and the need for care of children.
These are good reasons why we as members of this House should take a good look at this motion and support it as much as possible. We should move toward a bill of rights which would, to some extent, formalize our commitment to the ability of children to survive in Canada.
It is surprising that when we look around the country, we see a great deal of child poverty. In my home constituency of Saskatoon, there are something like 1,200 people who make use of the food bank every month. These kinds of things are common right across the country and most of the people affected by those kinds of situations are children. So, we do need to have a continuing commitment to the welfare of children. That is what this particular motion speaks toward.
Events of the last few years and the direction we have been going in human rights, the direction we have been going in the care and protection of individuals, particularly children, are overtaking us. The first League of Nations adopted a declaration concerning children 65 years ago, and that seems like a long time ago, yet we have not really been more specific in the direction we are taking since then.
The United Nations adopted a declaration of rights for the child 30 years ago. Ten years ago, we celebrated the International Year of the Child. This year, the United Nations General Assembly, after considerable negotiations, will be adopting a convention which I guess could be called a bill of rights in some ways.
We in Canada have played a considerable role in drafting and negotiating this particular convention. It is imperative that to make sure this direction is sustained, we in this House guarantee that what we think is good for the international child is good for the Canadian child
Private Members' Business
as well. Consequently, we must therefore clarify what we consider are the necessities for a bill of rights for children and move in that direction.
This motion attempts to clarify what should be considered part of what is necessary in a bill of rights for children. There is no doubt, as the previous speaker indicated, that there are jurisdictional problems as far as a charter of rights for children is concerned. Detailed negotiations are going to be required between the provinces and the federal government to achieve such a charter. It is imperative, therefore, that we begin these negotiations with the provinces as soon as possible so that when Canada does become the signatory to the United Nations convention, we can say truthfully and honestly that we are doing these things at home. Consequently, when we sign the convention, we will be able to say that what we believe is good for us is good for the other people of the world as well.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and support this private member's motion introduced by the member for Mission-Coquit-lan and seconded by the member for Oshawa that, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of negotiating with the provinces to provide a comprehensive bill of rights for children which would standardize laws throughout the country, and that this bill of rights include a child protection commission and an emergency hotline which children could contact in times of crisis.
Certainly the objectives of this private member's motion are very laudable indeed.
Although it has been 30 years now since the United Nations decided that children have rights, it was not until last spring that an international legal convention was drawn up to make these rights stick. It was only last November 21 that the United Nations General Assembly did pass and adopt this convention and it will be in this coming January that the ratification ceremony will take place. Thereafter, it will require some 20 states to ratify the convention and then it will be binding, as international law, on those signatories.
It is with pride that we should say that Canada played a vital role in the design of this convention. But if this code is adopted, countries will have to change their laws and

December 12, 1989
Private Members' Business
constitutions to comply with the convention, and certainly Canada is no exception.
It is easy to understand why it has taken so long to legalize the rights of children. Children do not have the right to vote, they do not have the political power, they are dependent on others for their well-being and, therefore, the responsibility on us is even greater.
During the Year of the Child 10 years ago, Poland stated that it was an appropriate time to establish a statement of children's rights with the power of law behind it. It took 10 years to draw up this convention. The United Nations General Assembly, as I said, just recently adopted it. Shall we allow Canada not to comply with it until 1991, as the former ambassador to the United Nations said it could take that long? We cannot allow that. I think we have a duty to act and to act promptly.
The guiding principle of this treaty is to promote the best interests of the child. I would add that it also protects the child from the moment of conception. The convention spells out a wide range of economic, social, civil, political and cultural rights for children. These include the right to an education, the right of minority children to practise their own culture and language, the right to be protected from exploitation, torture, maltreatment and the right of handicapped children to special services.
The 54 articles in the convention cover three major categories or areas: survival, protection and development. Although the convention sets out rights for children, it is truly directed at adults, for it is we adults who have the responsibility to ensure that these rights are truly respected and enshrined in a bill of rights.
The need for a bill of rights for children, both internationally and in Canada, to protect the lives and normal development of children is only too clear when one examines conditions that create injustice for children. It is imperative that in Canada, and indeed in the world at large, adverse conditions that create these injustices be addressed and addressed promptly.
It is not good enough to merely implement social services after damage has been done. I think it is important to mention some of the things which affect the well-being of children. These are: war, poverty, violence, abuse-physical, mental or emotional, trafficking in children, exploitation by the drug trade and malnutrition, especially under-nutrition. All of these factors can lead to illness and even to the death of children.
Canada is not immune. Millions of children die of chronic under-nutrition each year or grow up stunted in mind and body because there is not enough food for thousands of these children and also because their parents lack knowledge of health and nutrition. The single greatest killer of children is not war or malnutrition, it is dehydration through diarrhea. This is something that happens not only in Third World countries. Unfortunately, this still happens here in Canada. All that is necessary to avoid this is a solution of salt and sugar in water, but sometimes parents do not even make use of this or are not aware of this approach.
Children have a right to the highest attainable standard of health and access to medical services. This is something which should be protected not only through an international convention but through a bill of rights in Canada.
There are other issues affecting children. They include homelessness, education, child labour, and other health issues.
Let me refer to a fact sheet publication from A Choice of Futures: Canada's Commitment to its Children produced by a variety of organizations; the Canadian Child Welfare Association, the Canadian Council on Children and Youth, the Canadian Council on Social Development, the Canadian Institute of Child Health, the Child Poverty Action Group, Family Service Canada, and the Vanier Institute of the Family, institutions that truly are concerned about the welfare of children.
Six thousand children died in 1985 as a consequence of low birth weight, accidents and respiratory illnesses. Six hundred thousand children from birth to age 19 were hospitalized as a consequence, in the vast majority of instances, of respiratory illnesses. There are 275,000 disabled children between the ages of one and 14 in Canada, about 5 per cent of the child population. They are startling statistics in so far as the welfare or state of health of our children is concerned.
Canada's future will be determined by the children of today. In light of this, should we not have a bill of rights to protect our children, to ensure that they are adequately fed, that they are kept healthy, that they have access to an education? Protecting our children is imperative to maintaining the moral and ethical fabric of our advanced
December 12, 1989

democratic society. It is imperative to the economic future of our country. Most important, it is imperative to the well-being of the children themselves.
To address the bill more specifically it is important to have a comprehensive bill of rights for children as proposed in this private member's bill instead of different provincial legislation dealing with this issue. The children of Canada are entitled to standardized rights which will safeguard their access to educational services and to social programs uniformly from coast to coast. A Canadian child is a Canadian child whether he or she is a resident of Newfoundland, Winnipeg, or Vancouver. There is a need for a universal affordable day care program.
Motion C-254 states that the bill of rights for children should include a child protection commission. This would be a beneficial first step toward the establishment of a national child abuse strategy.
The number of incidents of child abuse, especially sexual abuse, in this country is staggering. This government has rejected criticism that it has not moved fast enough to counter this increasing problem. The Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated that the government has acted on the majority of recommendations of the 1984 report of the committee on sexual offences against children and youth. But the first recommendation of that report calls for the office of a commissioner, and that has yet to be established, and so I suggest that it be established.
It is obvious that we must co-ordinate federal and provincial efforts to bring about programs to aid in the prevention and treatment of child abuse. A child protection commission would be a necessary first step.
In conclusion, the government could prove its commitment to the children of Canada by passing this private member's motion. Not only would this benefit the children of our country, it would ensure that the International Convention for the Rights of Children is signed and ratified by Canada and that Canada's ratification is not blocked by the refusal of provincial ministers to agree to the convention.
Private Members' Business
Children are entitled to the same rights that adults have and it is the responsibility of adults, especially adults that are in government, to ensure that these rights are respected and protected. We need political will and leadership on behalf of children. We can fulfil our commitment to our nation's children by adopting this bill of rights so that we can start the federal-provincial negotiation on this issue and make our commitment to the children of Canada a living reality.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address this motion on the advisability of a comprehensive bill of rights for children which would standardize laws throughout the country and which would include a child protection commission and an emergency hotline for children.
The protection of children is one of the foremost duties of any society. We can only be as strong as our most vulnerable and weakest members. I therefore laud the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam for the concern she has shown for all children in Canada in her motion on this matter. Having said that, I would now like to turn my attention to some of the real difficulties faced by this motion.
Canada is under a federal system of government, with both levels of government, federal and provincial, having certain areas of responsibility under the Constitution. Provinces have been allocated power over much of family law, including the welfare of children. Section 92(13) of the Constitution Act of 1867 gives the provinces the right to legislate with respect to property and civil rights in the province. In the adoption reference, 1938, the Supreme Court of Canada determined inter alia that the welfare of children was a matter of provincial responsibility.
We have in Canada two basic types of legislation which afford protection to children; the criminal law which deals with the physical and sexual abuse of children, and child protection legislation which deals with the involvement of the state where a child has been abused or neglected. The federal government has constitutional jurisdiction over the former and the provincial governments have constitutional jurisdiction over the latter.
Provinces deal with child protection in a number of ways relevant to their individual circumstances and with a wide range of statutes covering such topics as adoption, child welfare, custody and access, and education. Each province has a government recognized body which has the responsibility for enforcing child welfare laws in

December 12, 1989
Private Members' Business
order to protect children and provide services to the child in his or her family. Given that these services are in place throughout this country, it does not seem to me to be advisable and necessary to involve the federal government in a long phase of negotiations to standardize these laws, removing flexibility from provincial legislatures and challenging the constitutional authority which has been in place since 1867.
Further, I am not at all convinced that a costly, central, monolithic child protection commission would or could provide better services than those now provided by each province and territory, nor am I persuaded that it would be constitutionally correct.
The hon. member has also included in her motion a reference to the need for an emergency hotline which children could contact in times of crisis. I would like to inform the House that the Canadian Children's Foundation has established a 1-800 number to serve just such a function. The number is 1-800-668-6868. It is called Kids Help Phone and it is my understanding that it is enjoying considerable success.
This crisis line handles calls from anywhere in Canada and refers children in distress to local authorities and services for assistance in dealing with their problems. This valuable service offers support and assistance to children from all across Canada. As a matter of fact, I spoke with Mrs. Heather Sproule of that agency recently. I might share with you a few statistics.
The crisis line was started in May of this year and already they have had some 75,000 calls. The average per day is about 800. On weekends they get as many as 1,000 calls. Unfortunately, they only have five lines now but with increased funding they hope to have ten. When it is fully operational they will likely be receiving as many as
200,000	calls a year.
The average age of the callers is between 11 and 14 years of age. They even have had over 100 calls from youths four years of age to seven years of age. I am told that 76 per cent of the callers are female, 24 per cent are male. I do not know the reason for that mix, perhaps it is the male ego not wanting to admit that they do need some help. Fifty per cent of the calls are from Ontario and that is partly because the start-up was there, but they will be advertising and communicating in all regions
of the country in order that they may be able to help. I believe the federal government has contributed about $1.3 million to this most worth-while agency and $650,000 of that is to be matched by other donors. We wish them every success.
Children are our most important asset and, as I mentioned earlier, our society will be judged by how well we protect them. There are, in addition to child protection laws, criminal laws which protect our children. In particular, this government can be proud of its legislative achievements in the area of child sexual abuse.
In January of last year Bill C-15 became law. This bill amended the Criminal Code and the Canada Evidence Act to better protect children and youth from sexual abuse by enacting measures to permit more young children to testily and provide more sensitive procedures for obtaining their evidence. In addition, new offences were created and certain outdated and confusing provisions of the Criminal Code were repealed.
The Department of Justice has supported this initiative through law information activity such as an easy to read booklet for children aged four to ten that tells them to tell someone if they have been sexually abused, and a booklet for adults telling them how to proceed if a child discloses an incident of sexual abuse to them.
Concern for children is expressed not only in the Criminal Code but in the federal government's family law legislation. The Divorce Act, for example, provides that custody of a child is to be decided upon a consideration of the child's best interest only. This makes it clear that the needs and rights of the child are the central and, indeed, the only concern of the courts when deciding the difficult question of custody of a child.
The government has expressed its concern in other ways for children in situations of divorce through the Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act. This act plays an important role in the enforcement of child support payments as well as the recovery of children wrongfully abducted from the custodial parent by the non-custodial parent. All too often, it is sad to say, the parent who is to pay support for the child, usually the father, economically abandons his child by
December 12, 1989

not paying or by paying late or by paying less than the ordered or agreed to amount.
The Federal Government Enforcement Assistance Act allows for the garnishment of designated federal funds to enforce delinquent support payments. I understand the program has been a tremendous success having intercepted a total of $6.3 million in the year prior to June 30, 1989. In many instances, the debtor father chooses to disappear rather then to pay child support. In such cases, the federal government will search its information banks in an effort to locate the father, thereby aiding provincial authorities in the enforcement of the support order or agreement.
In conclusion, information will also be released where a non-custodial parent takes a child contrary to an existing custodial arrangement. Information has been released in a total of 6,638 cases in the period from the establishment of the program on December 1, 1987, up to June of this year. The Federal Enforcement Assistance Act is part of a larger federal and provincial initiative to provide concrete assistance to children of divorcing families.
The government's work in the areas of support and custody and the Criminal Code are simply a few examples of our commitment to the protection of all Canadian children. The value of children cannot be overemphasized. They are the future of our country. This motion, however, fails, in my humble opinion, to significantly improve the lot of children in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to stand before you today and to address the motion focusing on children. I would like to commend the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam for bringing this matter before the House of Commons. Children are the cornerstone of this country, the basis for Canada's future.
The motion refers to a potential bill of rights for children, to a child protection commission and to a hotline; initiatives which are certainly diverse. But we must remember the other means by which we assist families and children. Their rights depend not only on
Private Members' Business
laws or organizations but as well on other very practical means of support.
Families are the first form for socialization of our children, for shaping and teaching the social values vital to the well-being of children. We therefore need to ensure a positive environment for families so that they, in turn, can fulfil their nurturing and caring responsibilities for our children.
Over the past 150 years, governments all across the world have undertaken specific measures to support families and their children. The recent international report from the United Nations to establish and adopt a convention on the rights of the child is certainly evidence of this.
Domestically, Canada has established a comprehensive approach to supporting families. An important feature of the Canadian system of support is the shared responsibility between federal and provincial jurisdictions. Constitutionally, provincial governments have prime responsibility for the well-being of children and through, for example, their social services and social assistance programs they discharge their responsibility. The federal government assists or facilitates these provincial activities largely through the transfer of moneys through programs such as the Canada Assistance Plan and Established Programs Financing.
From the federal government's perspective the concept of a family benefit related to the child goes back to 1918 when an amendment to the Income War Tax Act introduced the child tax exemption. The family allowance program then came into effect in 1945 demonstrating that Canada has accepted its obligation to assist in the upbringing of children. It was established as a vehicle whereby the federal government could supplement family income in order to alleviate some of the costs of caring and raising children.
Several changes have been made to family allowance since its inception in order to make the system of family benefits better targeted to families most in need.
Currently the federal government delivers almost $3 billion in family allowance benefits to over 3.5 million families on behalf of 6.5 million children. Benefits are paid, usually to the mother, on a monthly basis. In 1989 the monthly benefit is set at approximately $33 per child amounting to nearly $400 per year. Current federal

December 12, 1989
Private Members' Business
income support for families does not stop with family allowances. In this regard, family allowances are complemented by a system of child related benefits delivered largely through the personal income tax system.
The child tax credit program which benefits lower income families is another key source of income support for families. Since taking office in 1984 this government has significantly enhanced the maximum value of the credit by over 50 per cent, with the actual benefit increasing from $367 per child in 1984 to $565 per child in 1989. Family allowances and the basic child tax credit together support families and children by almost $1,000 per child annually.
As part of the recent child care initiative, the federal government also introduced in 1988 an additional supplement to the child tax credit in respect of children six years of age and under. The supplement is valued at $200 per child in 1989 and for subsequent tax years. The federal government has undertaken other income tax support measures to assist families with children. For example, we have proposed the new goods and services tax package which, when all elements are taken together, will mean that families with incomes of less than $30,000 per year will be better off than before the package had taken effect. As part of the package, families will benefit from an enhanced tax credit under the goods and services tax package which would be paid quarterly, in advance. The maximum value of the credit would be $275 per adult and $100 per child with special arrangements to support single parents.
Families will also benefit from a proposed reduction in the middle income tax bracket to somewhere in the order of 25 per cent. This rate reduction complements the enriched credit since the benefit it provides increases over the income range where the credit benefits are declining. We also assist parents with the cost and affordability of non-parental forms of child care. Through the personal income tax system, families are able to deduct up to $4,000 in work-related child care expenses in respect of pre-school age children and $2,000 in respect of school age children.
Through the Canada Assistance Plan, a cost-sharing program with the provinces, the federal government shares in eligible provincial expenditures on child care. In 1988-89 the federal government expected to spend
some $200 million under this cost-sharing program in respect of child care. The federal government intends to enhance its support for child care through a new national child care initiative which, as reported in both the Speech from the Throne and the Budget, will be introduced before the end of this mandate.
Families with new-born babies should soon experience additional support as the result of new legislation which is currently before the House and which would completely revise the current regime of maternity and sickness benefits.
The legislation will amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and introduce a multi-tiered system of maternity, parental and sickness benefits, including 15 weeks of maternity benefits available during the period surrounding the birth of a child; 10 weeks of parental benefits available to natural or adoptive parents, either the mother or the father, 15 weeks of sickness benefits and so on. The new unemployment insurance regime will allow claimants to receive each type of benefit up to its maximum as long as the cumulative duration of special benefits does not exceed 30 weeks.
In all of this, of course, we cannot forget that the best source of social protection is a job, and parents who have jobs are better able to provide for their own children. This federal government has been very successful in its economic policy efforts and has created over 1.5 million jobs since taking office in 1984.
Nonetheless, as we are all aware, family functioning sometimes breaks down as a result of outside strains and pressures. The federal government is concerned about these problems and with ensuring that families continue to be able to operate effectively and efficiently.
We are also aware of the important role that the public sector can play, both directly and indirectly, in assisting families during times of crisis. At the federal level, several initiatives have been introduced recently in support of families in crisis situations. For instance, we have identified and are responding to the priority issue of child abuse and, more generally, family violence.
In 1986, a five-year, $25 million initiative on child sexual abuse was announced. This initiative included the appointment of a special adviser on child sexual abuse, as we have already heard, who is expected to present his
December 12, 1989

report to the Minister of National Health and Welfare early in the new year.
A subsequent announcement in 1988 outlined a new $40 million family violence initiative. Under the second initiative, the majority of the funds, that is about $20 million, were allocated towards the creation of 500 new shelter units for battered women and their children.
The federal government is committed to undertaking further work in the area of family violence. To this end, we are developing a new family violence initiative which, in co-operation with provinces and the non-governmental sector, will improve the support available to families and children facing crisis and/or abusive situations.
The federal government has also eased the problems of marriage breakdown and divorce by introducing new divorce legislation which amended the grounds for divorce and humanized its consequences. To assist with the enforcement of support, the federal government also introduced services which provide for the release of information from designated federal banks to help locate persons who do not meet their obligations to a family order. They as well to provide for the garnishment of designated federal moneys from defaulting spouses.
Other federal initiatives in respect of families include efforts to reduce the problem of drug abuse in Canada and particularly among our young through the National Drug Strategy, and financial support to the provinces through the Established Programs Financing arrangements which supports the provision of health care in the education system.
The policies which I have just outlined are major federal programs which support families and children in Canada. These initiatives have helped families to cope with an ever-changing society by ensuring access to the key services and programs; child care, counselling, health care and education.
These initiatives have also contributed to lessening the problem of child poverty. In this regard, since 1984 the incidence of low income among children has continued to drop from a high of 20 per cent to just under 17 per cent in 1987.
Private Members' Business
We all have a vested interest in ensuring that today's children are provided with adequate social and health protection. I welcome this opportunity to speak on such a fundamental vital issue as our children.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently Canada joined all major countries in the world as a signator to the historic UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Canada, as a result, is legally obligated to adapt our policies and our legislation to reflect this convention as it applies particularly to protect the rights of children in Canada.
This motion we are debating today, which was sponsored by the member for Mission-Coquitlam, reinforces the UN convention by advocating a bill of rights for Canadian children. I commend her for her initiative. We hope this motion will be adopted not only by this House but by all provinces and by the Government of Canada as a guideline and commitment to protect the rights of Canadian children.
When we see the plight of starving children on TV, children from Africa with their bloated bodies and eyes that we cannot bear to look into, we are moved. But do we take action?
UNICEF reported at a conference I attended last summer that 40,000 children die each day from simple childhood diseases that are preventable. The cost of curing these diseases is minimal and yet do we contribute, as citizens, to save one child?
Today it was reported on the CBC that the UN predicts 100 million children may die in the next 10 years because of lack of nutrition and neglect. It is almost unbelievable that we live in this kind of a world.
However, in our concern for the world's children we must not forget our own children in Canada. The problems of many of Canada's children are hidden behind closed doors in our cities, towns and countryside. Child poverty, child abuse and child neglect are not visible. Yet, in Canada, well over one million children live below the poverty line. Children are the fastest growing users of food banks in this country.
Many of these children are disadvantaged from birth. Child mortality rates are twice as high in poor households as in the rest of the country. Babies are born underweight and face medical complications because of their mothers' poor nutrition during pregnancy. Young brains, as a result, do not develop and progress in school is difficult. Poor kids face a high dropout rate in high school, further limiting their options. Many become

December 12, 1989
Private Members' Business
homeless street kids in their teens, with all the dangers that lifestyle entails. Verbal, physical and sexual abuse of children also are on the rise. Many children who are sexually abused grow up to become prostitutes and patients in psychiatric hospitals, and we viewed this recently, in dramatic terms, in documentaries on television.
Canada was a signator to the UN convention on the rights of the child and we are morally bound to adhere to its precepts. Article 27 of this convention states that as a member nation we, as a signator, must ensure a standard of living adequate for children's physical, mental, spiritual, moral and social development.
While parents have the primary responsibility to provide security of life for their children, this is often not within their financial capacities. This means that where there are difficulties and where incomes are inadequate in families-and there are many, many of these, one in four children are in families who are in this situation- the state must supplement incomes and provide support programs. But we are not doing that in an adequate way. Sure, we have token welfare programs, but they are far below the minimum standard that is needed to sustain a family with young children.
I think that this government has short-changed us. Our children surely are our future, and our future is in trouble. Our society creates child poverty and neglect because it is based on inequalities. Women are left alone to raise children, without adequate incomes and without opportunities for independence in the future. Many parents are unemployed or underemployed. Housing is unaffordable for many young families today.
Our Conservative government leaves people at the mercy of the market-place where corporations reap profits while people lose jobs, and of course children suffer. Instead of improving social security and family benefits, the government's tax policies have increased the burden on low-income people.
What can we do to ensure that the rights of children are protected in Canada? We need a policy of full employment so that parents will be guaranteed a job with pay equity and parental leave provisions and affordable, quality child care. We need a children's bill of rights that
will be enforced by governments, and by the federal government in particular.
I support the motion of my hon. colleague for Mission-Coquitlam that this government should begin negotiating with the provinces to provide a children's bill of rights which will standardize laws throughout Canada. I also support her motion that this bill of rights should include a child protection commission and an emergency hotline which children could contact in times of crisis.
Why do we as Canadians and as world citizens tolerate the hardship that so many of our children are experiencing?
Because others profit by it.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
As my colleague says, because others profit by it. People on this side of this House, I hope, do not tolerate that. Why do we sit back in complacency knowing that a generation of children who should be the leaders and parents of the future are instead being scarred by poverty and abuse? How can we give at Christmas to assuage our guilt and then feel free to ignore and forget our children's poverty and the problems of the children of Canada for the rest of the year? Why does poverty continue to exist in an affluent country such as ours?
These are the questions we must answer with action. One of the first steps is for all of us to agree to adopt and implement a children's bill of rights.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join the list of many other speakers who have lent their voices to the important question of children's rights in Canada. I wish to thank the hon. member from Mission-Coquitlam for placing before the House of Commons her motion on this subject.
During the course of this debate on the issue of a comprehensive bill of rights for children, a number of speakers have alluded to the developments that have taken place internationally in regard to the human rights of the child. In fact, several members have suggested that as an alternative to elaborating a new bill of rights for children in Canada efforts in this country be focused on the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the

Child. I wish to express my support for this suggestion, which I believe is a realistic means to enhance protection in this country for our children.
During earlier stages of this debate when reference was made to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, it was with the knowledge that the convention had not been adopted in final by the UN General Assembly. That important step was in fact taken on November 20, 1989, when the General Assembly adopted the convention by consensus.
As a Canadian, I am proud of the leading role that this country played in both the drafting and adoption of this fundamental instrument. Now that it has been adopted, the process of examining the question of Canadian signature and ratification of the convention will commence.
As the debate on the motion before us has progressed, it has become increasingly clear that many, if not all, of the issues that would be included in the Canadian bill of rights for children are addressed in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Members speaking on this question have raised a number of extremely important concerns relating to the need for enhanced protection for children.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today on an issue which has been raised repeatedly
Adjournment Debate
by myself and other members for the last number of years. It is the issue of a safe drinking water act.
Last May 10,1 asked a question of the Minister of the Environment calling on him to act in a preventive way, for once, and to live up to this government's commitment to bring in a safe drinking water act.
The requests for this act have been more urgent than in previous years as people from Winnipeg, for example, have become alarmed, and rightly so, by the plans of Consolidated Professor Mining. This company has been testing the feasibility of opening a gold mine in Shoal Lake, Ontario, the source of Winnipeg's drinking water. They want to build this mine on Stevens Island in the middle of the lake. Their operation would involve the crushing of rocks, which contain arsenic, right on the island with the assurance, so they say, that none of the arsenic would make its way into the lake.
They say they have retaining ponds which will never, ever leak under any circumstances. We are told not to worry about their having arsenic so close to the intake for Winnipeg's water, because there will never be any accidents, nor will there ever be any spills. It reminds me of the assurances that I am sure the people of Ukraine got from the Soviet nuclear experts about the possibility of a reactor accident, or the assurances that the people of northern Saskatchewan got about the retaining ponds at Wollaston Lake and other places where we have had spills recently of uranium mining waste water into the natural environment there.
It does not take a great deal of wisdom and foresight to see that such an operation poses an absolutely unnecessary risk to the health of the people of Winnipeg. The response to this issue in Winnipeg has been strong. It has been led by the Winnipeg Water Protection Group and its president, Helen McCullough. I had the opportunity to meet with Helen last summer and subsequently on a number of other occasions. The research and effort that they have put into stopping this project has been remarkable and should be commended.
As well, I would like to commend three grade five students from John de Graff School in my riding who were concerned about this, perhaps concerned that the adult community was not doing enough. They gathered

December 12, 1989
Adjournment Debate
over 300 names on a petition about this issue. I had the honour of bringing their petition to the House last June. I commend them again for their actions.
These young people are right to be concerned that so far all that we have seen from the federal government on this issue is talk but no action. On May 10 the answer that I received from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who assured me that as a fellow Manitoban he shared my concern on this issue, stated, as reported at page 1541 of Hansard:
No approval should be given until every assurance has been given
that the water supply is safe.
This begs a question as far as I am concerned. Surely the government understands that the way to make sure that the water supply is safe is not to allow mines that leach arsenic to be built on islands in the middle of the lake in the first place. The way to do that is to bring in an act that ensures that commercial development such as this will always take a back seat to the safety of drinking water for Canadians. Surely if we have reached any point at all in our environmental consciousness we have reached the point where a gold mining company should not have a claim of any sort by which it could even think about establishing a good mine in the middle of the drinking water supply of 600,000 Canadians. Surely we should reach a point where that is not even on the table, that is not even an option, that is not even considered.
This is what I have in mind for a safe drinking water act. Such an act has been promised by the government in speeches and letters over and over again but the act has failed to materialize. My colleague from Beaches- Woodbine has been pushing for such an act for years, repeatedly bringing in Private Members' Bills to this effect. The government of the day, be it Liberal or Conservative, has always killed these bills at that stage.
Last June, Bill C-224, a safe drinking water act, was brought before the House by my colleague from Beaches-Woodbine and was talked out by a Liberal, the hon. member for Gander-Grand Falls. It is enough to make a person wonder if either the Liberals or the Conservatives will ever see the light as far as the safety of drinking water for Canadians is concerned.
We have been asking the government to take some initiative for years now. The government has been promising action but none has been seen.
In November, Helen McCullough received a disturbing letter from an Environment Canada official that told her the Shoal Lake management plan "has not directly involved Environment Canada to date". Why has it not? Why has it not, given all the assurances that we have received in this House from various federal ministers? Why has Environment Canada not been involved? What is the federal government doing with respect to this issue? Where is our safe drinking water act? The government has had years to move and the safety of as many as 650,000 people now is at stake. Why the reluctance to bring in the legislation?
This matter is clearly in the federal government's jurisdiction. It is time for the government to do something and not just talk about it.
I see that the hon. member for Brandon-Souris is preparing to respond on behalf of the government, someone who is also from Manitoba. Perhaps he will have some goods news for us, that for once this government will act in the interest of Manitobans. It did not with respect to Rafferty-Alameda. It got off to not a bad start. It did something right, but it has allowed that to lapse too.
Once again, in terms of the rhetoric of the government with respect to the environment, its bark has been a whole lot stronger than its bite. We would like to see some bite on Rafferty-Alameda, some bite on a safe drinking water act and some bite for the drinking water supply of Winnipegers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
If the hon. member will wait, I think he will find that there is some information here which applies to the question he has raised of the EARP process.
December 12, 1989

The Fisheries Act and the Navigable Waters Protection Act were the two acts that might have served this purpose. However, a recent decision by the Federal Court with regard to the Old Man River Dam in Alberta has cast doubt on the applicability of the EARP to the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
Under the Fisheries Act, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans may request plans and specifications for any project that is likely to result in the alteration, disruption or destruction of fish habitat, or in the deposit of a deleterious substance in water frequented by fish. While such a request may require the application of the EARP, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans does not consider the request to be justified in the specific circumstances of the Consolidated Professor Mine because the Ontario Environmental Assessment Act process will provide for the opportunity to address potential impacts on fish or fish habitat.
I wish to add that as a result of the expressions of concern by Winnipeg residents and as a result of discussions among the federal government, Ontario and the Province of Manitoba, Ontario decided to designate the proposed mine under its own Environmental Assessment Act. I understand the government of Manitoba is satisfied with the proposed review process. I can assure you that Environment Canada officials will also actively participate in the review of the project under the Ontario process.
The proposed mine is, as the hon. member probably knows, also subject to the federal metal mining liquid effluent regulations. Those regulations are rigorously applied.
With respect to the proposed federal safe drinking water act, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Hon. Perrin Beatty, has indicated that he intends to introduce a drinking water safety act that would establish drinking water quality objectives that would be mandatory within the federal domain. The proposed act would not directly address the issues that the hon. member has mentioned. It would permit the Department of National Health and Welfare to enter into agreements with other jurisdictions in order to solve drinking water problems of common interest. I think that is of considerable importance, Mr. Speaker.
Adjournment Debate HEALTH

Mr. Speaker, in May 1986 the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare produced a report on AIDS. The government responded by saying it was doing everything it could.
Two years later, in May of 1988, the Royal Society produced a report on AIDS. The government again responded by saying it was doing everything it could.
The former Minister of Health said in 1987 to the UN General Assembly: "In my opinion, we in Canada are doing our utmost to bring AIDS under control within our own borders." But AIDS groups and we in the opposition have said consistently that in fact the government was doing very little while this lawless fatal disease spread.
The current Minister of Health said he agreed with the opposition and recognized that his government had done virtually nothing to control the spread of AIDS. He said in The Medical Post on May 9, 1989: "I would have liked to have inherited a national strategy, but I didn't." He also said that affected groups are not being consulted. Looking at the way we have proceeded to date he said: "Too often the communications have not been adequate."
On August 11, 1988 the Prime Minister crowed over his government's AIDS policy saying it is part of a solid record of achievement of which all members of this Parliament can be proud. We on this side of the House have no pride in the inaction of this government, and apparently the Minister of Health is not part of his own government's action either.
Further, at the Montreal International Conference on AIDS, the Minister of National Health and Welfare in his speech talked about what his government was going to do in the future and did not indicate much about what the government had done in the past, and for good reason. The government's record on developing an AIDS strategy and responding to the AIDS crisis remains a record of inaction.
Five years ago when the Conservatives took office there were 122 cases of people living with AIDS. When I asked my question on AIDS in May there were 2,736 cases, an increase of 2,200 per cent in five years. Now there are in excess of 2,900 cases of people living with AIDS.

Adjournment Debate
In addition to this massive and tragic growth in people living with AIDS are those tens of thousands-perhaps
50,000	people-testing HIV positive.
AIDS is a preventive condition. Yet many problems remain in reducing its incidence. I would like to relate a few of those problems which the government has yet to address.
It is known how the HIV virus is spread, but there remains a great deal of ignorance and misapprehension about the virus and about AIDS in general. While some have changed their behaviour on the basis of the information available, others have not. Condoms are not as widely available as they should be. Needle exchange programs have been thwarted by some provinces. Persons with AIDS or who have tested HIV positive are frequently discriminated against. The federal government has been far too slow to react to show the leadership needed. The same goes for provincial governments in Canada.
Insufficient research on AIDS and the HIV virus is being conducted and access to promising new treatments is too often hindered. Governments at all levels have funded the fight against AIDS in a totally inadequate manner.
Early testing and diagnosis in the treatment of HIV infection is critical. Yet the lack of availability of anonymous testing facilities prevents many from coming forward for testing.
Faced with inadequate government funding, leadership and co-ordination, community groups which have performed so well in the fight against AIDS are often understaffed and underfunded. The federal Centre for AIDS has not acted in such a way as to have gained the confidence of those in the field.
All these problems with the fight against AIDS should be seen in the light of the continued increase in the number of people with AIDS in Canada and should be seen in the light of inadequate funding and leadership by this Conservative government. This is in sharp contrast to the situation in other countries. Australia is a good example of this. There the federal government has shown leadership in the development of an effective strategy dealing with AIDS, including consultation with support groups. In addition, on AIDS the Australian
government spends four times the per capita amount spent in Canada.
Canada has a long way to go and people are losing their future and, indeed, dying in the process. All the while this Conservative government sits back without taking leadership in policy development and a funding role.
Canada should have had a national AIDS strategy in place and in operation by now. There has been no valid excuse for the delay. The way ahead is clear. The strategy should deal with education and prevention, treatment, care and support, testing, cancelling discrimination and research. The government should develop a policy in the near future. It has an enormous amount of information available to it to do so.
In closing, if I may, I would like to pay particular tribute to all those working in support groups, voluntaiy and otherwise, for the very important work they are performing. They deserve and need the commitment and adequate funding which this government has not seen fit as yet to provide.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the Fifth International Conference on AIDS in Montreal the Minister of National Health and Welfare announced this government's commitment to develop a national strategy on AIDS by the end of the year.
The development of a national AIDS strategy is an exercise which requires the participation and the involvement of all those involved in the fight against AIDS. These include the federal, provincial and municipal governments, as well as the non-government organizations in the country. Discussions with the various agencies have been ongoing and will continue.
The strategy will delineate the appropriate objectives and propose a course of action over a medium term of five years and will require input from other federal departments which will include Justice, Secretary of State, Corrections, Treasury Board Secretariat, Employment and Immigration, Labour, CIDA, External Affairs, the Department of National Defence and the Solicitor General.
The strategy will also be developed through a series of bilateral discussions and consultations. These will provide a forum for the exchange of information and activities already under way at the federal and provincial
December 12, 1989

levels in areas of education and community-based public awareness initiatives.
Ongoing consultations with the non-governmental sector are being conducted in parallel with the above process in order to obtain their input for the formulation of the national AIDS strategy.
Consultations have been held with such groups as the Canadian Public Health Association, the Canadian AIDS Society and their affiliates, the Canadian Haemophilia Society, the Canadian Council on Social Development, the scientific community and representatives from the educational field, including groups such as the Council of Ministers of Education, Canadian Home and School and Parent Teacher Federation, the Canadian Teachers Federation and others. The success of the development of a national strategy depends on the participation of all the partners.
The development of a national strategy on aids is a
Adjournment Debate
complex and important step in the fight against this deadly disease. It is crucial that we have adequate consultation with all the partners if we are to achieve a truly national approach. It is expected that the complete and comprehensive national strategy will be announced in the first half of 1990.
